WHAT TO DO AFTER A

California Car Accident

Knowing what to do next can protect your health, your rights and your claim. Here are the key steps.

QUICK LINKS

CALIFORNIA CAR ACCIDENT GUIDE

What to do after a California car accident

  1. 1

    Get to safety and request help.

    Move to a safe location if possible and call 911 so emergency services can respond.

  2. 2

    Get appropriate medical attention.

    Even if you feel fine, some injuries don’t show up right away. A medical evaluation creates a record of your condition.

  3. 3

    Exchange information when safe.

    Share your name, contact details, insurance information and vehicle details with the other driver, but avoid admitting fault or making statements about the accident.

  4. 4

    Preserve photos, footage and witness details.

    Take clear photos of the scene, your vehicle and any visible damage. If there are witnesses, get their names and contact information.

  5. 5

    Notify your insurer promptly.

    Report the accident to your insurance company as soon as possible, but keep your description factual and avoid speculation.

  6. 6

    Check reporting requirements and deadlines.

    Depending on the severity of the crash, you may need to file a report with the California Highway Patrol or your local police department.

What compensation may be available?

Every category requires evidence. Recovery depends on the facts and applicable law.

Medical expenses

Necessary treatment and supported future care.

Lost earnings

Pain and emotional distress

How the injury affects daily life.

Understand your take-home recovery

Settlement value differs from what you receive after attorney fees, case expenses and applicable liens.

What if you were partly at fault?

Compensation may be reduced by your share of responsibility. For example, 20% responsibility means a 20% reduction before other adjustments.

What if the driver has no insurance?

Review uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, medical payments and collision coverage. Policy terms and limits apply.

WHY TRUCK ACCIDENT CLAIMS ARE DIFFERENT

Why truck accident claims are different

Truck crashes involve unique factors, from federal regulations to complex liability. Here’s what matters.

QUICK LINKS

TRUCK ACCIDENT CLAIMS

What Evidence Matters in a California Truck Accident Claim?

The right evidence can show what happened, who was responsible, and how the crash caused your injuries. Here’s what to look for — and how it fits into your claim.

KEY TYPES OF EVIDENCE

Driver Logs

May show driving time, duty periods and rest.

Vehicle Data

May contain speed or braking information, depending on the system.

Video and Dispatch

May show events, trip instructions and timing.

Maintenance Records

May show inspections, reported defects and repairs.

Cargo Records

May help explain loading and securement.

Different records, different questions

Driver logs track duty and rest. Vehicle data may record speed or braking. Availability varies.

Preserve relevant evidence early

Covered carriers retain duty records for at least six months from receipt of the records. Other evidence may be unavailable sooner. 49 CFR 395.8.

FATIGUE RULES AND JURISDICTION

Which trucking rules apply?

Federal and California intrastate rules depend on the operation and applicable exceptions. An electronic log does not mean federal driving-hour limits always apply. Carriers also have duties to inspect, repair and maintain vehicles and to secure cargo against shifting.

FMCSA hours rules CHP intrastate guidance Federal maintenance rules

LEGAL GUIDANCE

Who may be responsible?

The driver, employer, carrier, repair provider, cargo handler or manufacturer may be examined when facts and law support a claim. No company is automatically liable.

AFTER A TRUCK ACCIDENT

What to Do After a California Truck Accident

The moments after a truck accident are overwhelming, but the steps you take can protect your health, your rights and your claim.

6 ESSENTIAL STEPS

  1. 1. Seek Safety & Emergency Help

    Move to a safe location if you can. Call 911 for medical assistance and report the accident.

  2. 2. Obtain Medical Care

    Get checked by a medical professional, even if you feel fine. Some injuries aren’t immediately obvious.

  3. 3. Photograph Truck & Trailer Identifiers

    When it is safe, capture the truck, trailer, license plates, DOT numbers and any visible damage.

  4. 4. Save Original Media & Witnesses

    Keep original photos, videos, receipts and notes. Get contact information for any witnesses.

  5. 5. Keep Report & Insurance Information

    Obtain the police report number and share insurance information with the proper parties.

  6. 6. Check Deadlines

    Know the time limits for reporting, claims and lawsuits. They can be shorter than you think.

Do Not Enter Traffic or Approach Spilled Cargo

Stay out of traffic lanes, avoid the truck and never approach spilled or leaking cargo to collect evidence. It can be dangerous, unstable and may involve hazardous materials.

DMV REPORTING REQUIREMENT

DMV reporting: within 10 days

An SR-1 is generally required if anyone is injured or killed, or property damage exceeds $1,000. It is separate from a police or insurance report.

California DMV SR-1 guidance

STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS

Check your filing deadlines

Personal injury lawsuitUsually 2 years from injury
California state or local government injury claimGenerally 6 months

Exceptions and additional deadlines apply. These are general rules, not a calculation of your deadline.

RIDER QUESTIONS

Lane splitting, fault and helmet use

Lane splitting is legal in California.

It does not automatically establish fault. Vehicle movements, speed, visibility and road conditions still matter. Riding on the shoulder is not lane splitting.

CHP lane-splitting guidance

What if I was partly at fault?

California comparative-fault rules can reduce compensation by your share of responsibility. An insurer allegation is not a final determination.

California jury instruction CACI 405

How does helmet use affect a claim?

California requires compliant helmets for riders and passengers. A disputed helmet issue requires reviewing the injuries and whether the alleged conduct contributed to the harm.

California Office of Traffic Safety

CALIFORNIA ACCIDENT RESOURCES

California Accident Claim Deadlines

Know the steps. Check the dates that matter.

The time you have depends on the claim, who may be responsible, and what has already been filed. Many California accident injury lawsuits have a two-year filing period. A claim involving a government agency can require action within six months—and a rejection notice can start a separate deadline.

Received a government notice or concerned a deadline has passed?

Keep the notice and envelope together and seek a prompt review. Call MMG Law Firm at (818) 539-7969 or request a free case evaluation. Sending an inquiry does not pause a deadline or, by itself, establish an attorney-client relationship.

IN THIS GUIDE

COMMON STARTING POINTS

Different claims. Different deadlines.

General rules; your facts and claim type matter.

  • 2 years

    Private-party injury lawsuit

    Usually from the injury date.

  • 3 years

    Private-party property damage

    Usually from the damage date.

  • 6 months

    Government claim presentation

    Generally from accrual; a lawsuit comes later.

Exceptions apply. A claim is different from a lawsuit.

California accident deadlines at a glance

These are general starting points for common negligence claims, not a calculation of your filing date. “Accrual” means the point when the legal claim arises; it is often the injury date, but exceptions can change that analysis.

CLAIM OR STEPGENERAL TIME LIMITWHAT MATTERS
Injury lawsuit against a private driver or businessUsually two years from injuryIdentify each potential defendant and any exception.
Lawsuit for vehicle or other personal-property damage against a private partyUsually three years from damageThe longer property deadline does not extend an injury deadline.
Required claim to a California state or local public entity for injury, death, or personal-property damageGenerally six months from accrualPresent the claim to the proper entity using the required procedure.
Lawsuit after a government rejection notice that complies with the lawGenerally six months from personal delivery or mailing of the noticeThe date you open or read the letter is not the statutory starting point.
Government lawsuit when no legally compliant written rejection notice is givenGenerally two years from accrual, subject to applicable exceptionsThis does not eliminate the earlier claim-presentation requirement. Later notices must be reviewed.

The ordinary injury and property periods are summarized in the California Courts deadline guide. Government claim presentation is addressed in Government Code section 911.2, and the separate lawsuit periods appear in section 945.6.

Do not treat six months as 180 days. Calendar rules, triggering events, holidays, service methods, and special statutes need to be checked before selecting an exact date.

An insurance claim is different from a lawsuit

Opening an insurance claim, sending medical bills, or discussing settlement generally does not replace filing a lawsuit on time. A police report, DMV report, or complaint to a government office also does not automatically satisfy a required government damages claim.

If an adjuster says the file remains open, ask what that means for the legal deadline. Do not assume ongoing negotiations, continued treatment, or a verbal assurance gives you extra time. A possible extension, tolling agreement, or other exception needs its own legal review.

California Courts explains how an injury case proceeds in its personal injury guide. The goal is to preserve the right to pursue the case while the injuries and evidence are still being evaluated.

Government claims involve separate steps

A collision involving a city vehicle, public transit, a government employee acting within the scope of employment, or an allegedly dangerous public roadway may raise public-entity issues. A private driver and a government entity can have different deadlines arising from the same crash.

1Identify the entity and present the claim

For covered injury, death, and personal-property claims, the general presentation period is six months from accrual. Confirm the responsible entity, the required recipient, the claim contents, and the accepted submission method. Save the completed claim and proof of presentation.

The California Courts government-claim guide explains how to locate forms and submission information. The Department of General Services filing page is a starting point for State of California claims; it is not the universal filing office for cities, counties, or transit agencies.

2Track the response and every notice

A public entity generally has 45 days to act on a presented claim. Amendments and written extensions can change that schedule. If the entity does not act within the applicable period, the claim is generally deemed rejected. See Government Code section 912.4.

Save every response, mailing envelope, delivery record, and agreement. A notice about a late claim is not necessarily the same as a rejection of a timely claim.

3Review the deadline to sue

A written rejection that meets the statutory notice requirements generally starts a six-month lawsuit period when personally delivered or placed in the mail. If no compliant written notice is given, section 945.6 generally supplies two years from accrual, with applicable exceptions and adjustments.

Do not assume silence guarantees two years: a later compliant notice can affect the deadline. Missing the initial claim requirement is also a separate problem. Have the actual notice and claim history reviewed, rather than relying on the letter's heading alone. See Government Code section 945.6.

If the six-month government claim period was missed

Act promptly. There may be a procedure to request permission to present a late claim. Under Government Code section 911.4, the application generally must be presented within a reasonable time, not exceeding one year from accrual, with statutory exceptions in how that period is counted. It must explain the delay and include the proposed claim.

This is not an automatic extra six months. Timeliness, the reason for the delay, and the applicable grounds for relief all matter. Minority, incapacity, death, or qualifying mistake or excusable neglect can require particular facts and proof.

If the late-claim application is denied or deemed denied, a court petition for relief generally has its own six-month deadline. If the court grants that relief, section 946.6 requires the lawsuit within 30 days afterward. These are different procedural steps. A rejection letter should be reviewed to identify which step it concerns. See Government Code section 946.6.

Important exceptions and situations to flag

A child was injured

For many private-party injury claims, minority can pause the lawsuit limitation period. The public-entity rules differ: do not wait until the child turns 18 to investigate a government claim. Code of Civil Procedure section 352 expressly excludes covered government claims from its ordinary tolling rule. Separate late-claim relief may be available under specific conditions. See section 352 and the government relief provisions above.

An injury or its cause was discovered later

Delayed discovery can affect when some claims accrue. The analysis includes when the problem was discovered and when reasonable diligence should have revealed it. A later diagnosis or learning the full cost of an injury does not automatically restart the clock. Keep the medical timeline and explain what was known when. See the California Courts explanation of discovery and tolling.

The injured person lacked legal capacity

Statutory incapacity rules can affect some deadlines, but being in pain, receiving treatment, or being unable to work is not automatically the same as lacking legal capacity. Government late-claim relief has its own rules. Preserve medical records and the dates of any guardianship or conservatorship. See Code of Civil Procedure section 352 and Government Code section 946.6.

A person died, or a federal vehicle was involved

A fatal collision may involve both wrongful-death and survival claims. Death of a potential defendant can also raise separate estate procedures. Provide all relevant dates rather than assuming the ordinary injury timeline answers every question.

Claims involving a federal employee, such as certain postal-vehicle collisions, use a different process from California state and local claims. The U.S. Department of Justice explains federal administrative presentation, the generally applicable two-year presentation period, and the need to state a specific dollar amount in its Federal Tort Claims Act forms guidance. A separate federal lawsuit deadline may follow; do not apply the California table to a federal claim.

Insurance, reporting, and evidence have other timelines

Notify your insurer promptly and review the policy. Uninsured- and underinsured-motorist matters can involve special notice, suit, settlement, or arbitration requirements. A claim number alone does not establish that those requirements have been met. See the California Department of Insurance auto guide.

A DMV accident report is separate from a damages claim or lawsuit. The DMV requires an SR-1 within 10 days when the crash causes an injury, death, or more than $1,000 damage to any one person's property. See the DMV financial-responsibility guidance.

Evidence can disappear before a legal deadline expires. Save original photos and video, witness details, vehicle information, letters, and medical records. For commercial-truck crashes, some covered electronic driving records need be retained only six months; that is a record-retention rule, not your filing deadline. See FMCSA electronic logging guidance.

What to bring for a deadline review

You do not need a complete file before asking for help. Start with what you have:

  • The accident date, location, and report number.
  • Names of drivers, companies, public agencies, and insurers involved.
  • The injured person's age and any relevant dates of incapacity or death.
  • Copies of government claims, submission receipts, and all responses.
  • Rejection letters with envelopes, mailing dates, and delivery records.
  • Insurance policies, claim letters, settlement communications, and any arbitration documents.
  • Any lawsuit papers, court orders, or written deadline agreements.

Open the printable deadline-review worksheet. It helps organize information; it does not calculate a legal deadline.

Questions people ask before contacting MMG

Can I wait until medical treatment ends?

Do not assume treatment extends the deadline. An ongoing medical evaluation and the steps needed to preserve a claim can proceed on different schedules.

What if the insurer is still negotiating?

Keep negotiating communications, but have the filing date checked separately. Do not rely on an open insurance file as proof of an extension.

What if I think I am already too late?

Gather the dates and notices for prompt review. An exception or relief procedure may apply, but there is no assurance that a missed deadline can be fixed. Further delay may eliminate an available option.

Does contacting MMG protect the deadline?

No. Calling, emailing, or submitting an inquiry does not itself file a claim or lawsuit or stop a clock. Ask whether MMG has agreed to handle the matter and which filing responsibilities it is undertaking. If time is close, make the known date clear when you call.

How an Accident Claim Works in California

Understand the steps, your decisions, and what may happen next.

Stages can overlap. Not every claim requires a lawsuit.

IN THIS GUIDE

Know what happens next.

An accident claim usually begins with questions: Who may be responsible? What evidence is available? Which insurance applies? What will this cost, and will I have to go to court?

This guide explains the main stages for California car, truck, and motorcycle injury claims: consultation, investigation, negotiation, litigation when needed, and resolution. Some claims settle without a lawsuit. Others require court proceedings, and settlement discussions can continue while a lawsuit is underway.

  1. 01

    Consultation

    Review the crash, deadlines, fees, and next steps.

  2. 02

    Investigation

    Gather evidence, review coverage, and document injuries and losses.

  3. 03

    Negotiation

    Evaluate offers and the terms of a possible settlement.

  4. 04

    Litigation, if needed

    File a lawsuit, exchange evidence, and prepare for trial if needed.

  5. 05

    Resolution

    Address payment, expenses, reimbursement claims, and distribution.

You can ask for help before your file is complete. Call MMG Law Firm at (818) 539-7969 or request a free case evaluation. Tell us about any upcoming date, government notice, or court paper. An inquiry alone does not establish representation or pause a deadline.

The claim process at a glance

STAGEWHAT THE WORK INVOLVESYOUR PART
1. ConsultationReview the crash, possible claims, deadlines, and representation termsExplain what happened, bring available records, and ask about fees
2. InvestigationIdentify responsible parties, coverage, evidence, injuries, and lossesPreserve originals and provide accurate updates and documents
3. NegotiationPresent the claim, evaluate responses, and discuss settlement termsConsider advice and decide whether to accept a proposed settlement

These stages can overlap. A filing deadline may require a lawsuit before treatment or negotiations are complete. Not every claim reaches every stage, and a claim may end without a recovery. The California Courts civil-case overview explains the court process and why some cases resolve before trial.

1. Consultation: understand your options

An initial evaluation focuses on the collision, injuries, available records, possible defendants, and time limits. It also helps determine whether the firm can take the matter. A consultation is not a promise of representation, compensation, or a particular outcome.

Bring what you have: the accident date and location, photographs, report number, insurance information, medical-provider names, and letters or offers you received. Say whether a public vehicle, commercial truck, work activity, child, or fatal injury is involved. Missing documents can be identified during the discussion.

Before hiring a lawyer, understand the scope of the work and who will handle it. Ask how to send records, how updates will be communicated, and which decisions need your approval.

Review fees and expenses before proceeding

MMG's contingency rates vary by case stage. The written agreement explains the applicable percentage, when it changes, and how fees and expenses affect the recovery. MMG advances case expenses without an upfront payment. If there is no recovery, you owe MMG no attorney fees or case expenses. Medical bills, liens, and other third-party obligations are separate.

Ask whether the percentage is calculated before or after costs and which services are included. The State Bar's fee-agreement guidance explains why these details matter. Its discussion of expenses describes general arrangements; MMG's confirmed no-recovery expense policy is stated above.

2. Investigation: build the factual record

An investigation addresses responsibility, the connection between the crash and the injuries, the losses claimed, and possible sources of payment. Depending on the case, work may include obtaining reports, interviewing witnesses, reviewing photographs and video, identifying insurance, and consulting appropriate experts.

Evidence needs differ. A truck collision may call for driver, vehicle, maintenance, or business records. A motorcycle claim may involve road conditions, visibility, damaged protective equipment, and witness accounts. A report or insurance decision is one part of the evidence; neither automatically resolves every legal issue.

Preserve records and document the effect on your life

Keep original photographs, video, messages, letters, receipts, and damaged items when practical. Tell your lawyer about nearby cameras or evidence at risk of being overwritten. Discuss preservation needs before authorizing disposal or repairs, while also addressing storage charges and practical necessities.

Provide accurate medical and employment information, including relevant prior injuries. Keep bills, treatment instructions, work restrictions, pay records, and a factual record of how the injury affects daily activities. Medical decisions belong with qualified healthcare professionals; a claim should not dictate unnecessary care.

Future care or lasting limitations may need further evaluation. That does not mean every task must wait until treatment ends. Evidence preservation and legal deadlines can require immediate attention. See the California Courts personal-injury guide for the role of evidence in an injury case.

Understand which insurer is involved

Your insurer and another party's insurer may have different roles. Policy duties, available coverage, limits, exclusions, and reimbursement rights need review. A claim involving uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage can have additional requirements.

Your own policy may require cooperation, documents, or a statement. Before a recorded interview, broad authorization, or release, understand the request and discuss its scope with your lawyer. Do not ignore insurer communications. The California Department of Insurance accident guide explains claim investigation and policy responsibilities.

3. Negotiation: evaluate offers and tradeoffs

A settlement demand typically explains the basis of the claim, the supporting evidence, and the compensation requested. The insurer or other party may seek additional information, dispute responsibility or damages, deny coverage, or make an offer. Sending a demand does not guarantee payment or stop a filing deadline.

An offer should be considered alongside the evidence, disputed issues, available coverage, expected further costs, and the risks and time involved in continuing. Ask for an explanation of what remains uncertain and how the proposed terms affect you.

You decide whether to settle

Your lawyer advises you, but the decision whether to settle belongs to you or the person legally authorized to act for the claimant, subject to any required court approval. California's professional rules require lawyers to honor the client's settlement decision and communicate written settlement offers. See State Bar Rules 1.2 and 1.4.1.

Before accepting, ask what claims and parties the release covers, whether other coverage or claims could be affected, and what the estimated net payment would be. A release may give up rights even if additional problems appear later. Read and understand the terms before agreeing.

Mediation can help the parties reach agreement

In mediation, a neutral mediator helps the parties discuss a resolution. The mediator does not decide who wins or impose a settlement. Arbitration is different: an arbitrator can make a decision, and the consequences depend on the applicable agreement and rules. See California Courts' dispute-resolution guide.

4. Litigation: what happens if a lawsuit is needed

A lawsuit may be appropriate when the dispute cannot be resolved on acceptable terms or a filing deadline requires action. Starting litigation does not guarantee a trial or a recovery. It creates a court case with formal procedures, deadlines, and obligations.

Filing and service

The complaint identifies the defendants, allegations, and requested relief. Required papers must be filed and properly served. The defendants can respond, and the court manages the case. Government claims may require a separate administrative step before suit. The California Courts filing overview explains these stages.

Discovery and case preparation

Discovery is the formal exchange of information and evidence. It can include written questions, document requests, sworn testimony at a deposition, and subpoenas for records. An examination may be requested under applicable rules. You may need to help locate records, review responses for accuracy, and attend a deposition. Your lawyer can explain the procedure and prepare you to answer truthfully. See California Courts' discovery guide.

Motions can resolve legal issues or affect what evidence will be considered. Settlement conferences and negotiations may continue. If the case proceeds to trial, preparation includes witnesses, exhibits, expert issues, and the legal rules governing the evidence. See the California Courts trial-preparation guide.

Trial and what may follow

If the case is not resolved earlier, a judge or jury decides the issues submitted for trial. The outcome may include no recovery. After judgment, post-trial motions, an appeal, or collection issues can affect what happens next. A judgment is not the same as cash received; the court does not collect the money for you. See California Courts' judgment-collection guidance.

5. Resolution: understand the payment and accounting

When a settlement is reached, its terms must be documented and the required closing steps completed. Depending on the matter, these can include releases, court approval, dismissal papers, payment processing, and addressing claims against the recovery. Settlements involving minors can require court approval; California Courts provides minor-compromise forms and guidance.

The settlement amount and your net recovery differ

Ask for an itemized explanation showing the gross recovery, the agreed attorney fee, case expenses, applicable medical or reimbursement payments, any amount held for an unresolved issue, and the amount payable to you. Do not compare offers using only the headline number.

Health coverage does not necessarily eliminate reimbursement obligations. For example, Medi-Cal's Personal Injury Program may seek reimbursement for related services, and Medicare explains its conditional-payment recovery process. Whether a claim is valid, how much is due, and whether a reduction is available require review; reductions are not guaranteed.

Payment timing depends on the actual terms and outstanding steps. Any holdback should be explained. An unresolved issue does not justify holding every dollar indefinitely: State Bar Rule 1.15 addresses written accounting and prompt distribution of undisputed funds that the client or another person is entitled to receive.

How long does an accident claim take?

There is no dependable single timeline for every case. The next milestone is often more useful than a promised finish date.

WHAT AFFECTS TIMINGA USEFUL QUESTION TO ASK
Medical information and future needsWhat information is still needed to evaluate the injury?
Missing records or disputed factsWhich records are outstanding, and what can I help provide?
Multiple parties or coverage questionsWho may be responsible, and which coverage issues remain?
Negotiation or mediationHas an offer been made, and what decision is needed?
Court scheduling and discoveryWhat is the next court event or response deadline?
Payment, liens, or required approvalWhat is preventing distribution, and what happens next?

Negotiation and medical treatment do not automatically extend filing deadlines. Many private-party injury lawsuits generally have a two-year limit. Covered California government injury claims generally require presentation within six months, with separate later lawsuit deadlines and exceptions. Check your facts promptly using the California Courts deadline guide and government-claim guide.

Questions to bring to your consultation

  • What facts, evidence, or deadlines need attention first?
  • What work would MMG handle, and who will be my contact?
  • What fee applies at each case stage, and how are expenses deducted?
  • What documents should I preserve or send, and how should I send them?
  • What decisions will I need to make, and what is the next milestone?
  • If an offer arrives, how will we evaluate the release and estimated net recovery?

Common questions about the process

Does making a claim mean I am suing someone?

No. An insurance claim requests benefits or payment through an insurer. A lawsuit is a court proceeding. A settlement can resolve a claim before or after a lawsuit is filed.

Do I have to accept the first offer?

You can evaluate the proposal with legal advice before deciding. Consider its terms, any response deadline, the available evidence, and the risks of continuing. Neither rejecting nor accepting an offer guarantees a better outcome.

Will hiring a lawyer mean I have nothing else to do?

Your participation still matters. Provide accurate information, preserve records, keep contact details current, and respond to requests. If litigation requires testimony or other participation, discuss preparation and practical needs with your lawyer.

Can I contact MMG without the police report or all my bills?

Yes. Start with the details and records available. Make any known deadline or notice clear. Do not assume a submitted form means the firm has accepted the case or filed anything for you.

Compensation Available After a California Accident

IN THIS GUIDE

Document the full effect of your accident.

Compensation depends on your losses, supporting evidence, and applicable rules.

  1. 01

    Medical expenses

    Reasonable costs of necessary care, with support for future treatment.

  2. 02

    Lost income

    Missed earnings and supported changes in earning ability.

  3. 03

    Pain and daily life

    Physical discomfort, emotional harm, and lasting limitations.

An accident can create losses that continue long after the vehicle is repaired. Depending on the facts and applicable law, an injury claim may seek compensation for medical care, lost earnings, future losses, pain, and other harm caused by the accident.

A useful review identifies each loss, the evidence supporting it, and any legal or coverage limits. Listing a category does not mean it is recoverable in every case.

Compensation categories at a glance

CATEGORYWHAT MAY BE CONSIDEREDRECORDS TO KEEP
Medical expensesReasonable costs of necessary accident-related careProvider records, bills, payment explanations
Lost earningsIncome lost because of the injuryPay records, employer information, missed-work dates
Future lossesSupported future care and reduced earning abilityPrognosis, work restrictions, relevant expert assessments
Household servicesLost ability to perform customary household workTasks affected, time involved, help received
Pain and life impactPhysical pain, emotional distress, impairment, and lost enjoymentAccurate notes, treatment records, observations
Property damageVehicle or other property damage and qualifying loss of usePhotographs, estimates, receipts, valuation documents

California Courts explains that injury claims can address financial and emotional harm, including ongoing and future effects. Proof and legal responsibility remain essential. California Courts: Personal injury cases.

Medical expenses: past care and supported future treatment

Medical compensation concerns care connected to the injury, not simply the total printed on every bill.

California's medical-expense instruction addresses the reasonable cost of reasonably necessary care. Future care must be supported as reasonably certain to be needed. Treatment may include emergency services, consultations, rehabilitation, medication, or other appropriate care, depending on the evidence. Judicial Council: CACI 3903A, medical expenses.

Keep bills together with records showing the treatment provided. Insurance payment explanations can help distinguish charges, payments, adjustments, and remaining obligations. Ask which amounts are being used in the claim and why.

For future treatment, useful questions include: What care is expected? How often? For how long? What evidence supports its cost? A possible procedure mentioned in passing is different from a supported future-care need.

Practical step: Share provider recommendations accurately. Make healthcare decisions with qualified professionals. Additional treatment does not automatically increase compensation.

Lost income and reduced earning ability

Past lost earnings concern income you missed because of the injury. Future lost earnings concern income you are reasonably certain to miss later. Reduced earning capacity addresses an injury’s effect on your ability to earn.

These concepts overlap, so the same future loss should not be counted twice. A person does not necessarily need an established work history to have an earning-capacity claim; the evidence still must support the loss. Judicial Council: CACI 3903D, lost earning capacity.

Useful records include:

  • Pay statements and employment information.
  • Dates, hours, and duties you could not work.
  • Medical work restrictions and changes to your schedule.
  • Business records if you are self-employed.
  • Information about lasting limitations affecting your work.

Self-employment revenue is not automatically the same as lost income. Explain cancellations, replacement help, expenses, and how the injury affected the business so the loss can be evaluated accurately.

Practical step: Keep a dated work-loss record. Tell the lawyer whether you used paid leave or returned with modified duties rather than assuming those details are irrelevant.

Future losses need evidence

Future losses can be important when an injury has lasting consequences. An evaluation may need medical, vocational, or economic evidence to establish what is expected and how it should be valued.

Future economic damages may require a present-value calculation: money paid today to address losses occurring later. This differs from the treatment of future noneconomic harm. Judicial Council: CACI 3904A, present cash value.

Before considering a settlement, ask:

  • What future care or work limitations are supported?
  • Which needs remain uncertain?
  • Does the evaluation account for those uncertainties?
  • How would the release affect a later request for compensation?

Do not assume you can reopen a settled injury claim when additional treatment becomes necessary. Review the actual release and expected needs before deciding.

Household help and loss of household services

An injury can interfere with cooking, cleaning, caregiving, or other work you customarily perform at home. California recognizes a category for the lost ability to provide household services, with proof of their reasonable value and the services you would otherwise have provided. Judicial Council: CACI 3903E, household services.

Keep notes about the tasks affected, how often you performed them, and who helped after the accident. Preserve receipts when you hire assistance. Mention unpaid family help too, so its relevance can be reviewed.

Avoid counting the same assistance as both household-service loss and a separate care expense without examining the overlap.

Practical step: Describe what changed in concrete terms, such as needing help with weekly shopping or being unable to carry laundry upstairs.

Pain, emotional distress, and changes in daily life

Where legally available, noneconomic damages address harm that does not come with a simple invoice: pain, emotional distress, physical impairment, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life.

California's instruction does not prescribe a fixed formula. The evaluation depends on evidence and judgment, with future harm requiring appropriate support. Judicial Council: CACI 3905A, pain and suffering.

An injury may affect sleep, mobility, relationships, recreation, or independence. The useful question is how your life changed, for how long, and what evidence helps explain that change.

Practical step: Keep brief, honest notes about significant limitations. Share accurate symptoms and history with your healthcare providers. Avoid exaggeration and do not treat every ordinary frustration as an accident-related loss.

Vehicle damage, belongings, and loss of use

An accident may also damage your vehicle, helmet, riding gear, or other property. Keep photographs, repair estimates, receipts, and information about the item’s condition before the collision.

Property compensation has its own valuation rules. Repair costs, changes in value, and applicable policy terms require review; the original purchase price is not automatically the recoverable amount. Judicial Council: CACI 3903J, personal-property damage.

Loss-of-use questions may arise when damaged property cannot be used. Preserve transportation or rental records and ask whether the expense, duration, and applicable claim rules support recovery.

The Department of Insurance explains collision, liability, rental-reimbursement, and other coverage categories. Coverage under your own policy and damages claimed from another party can follow different rules. California Department of Insurance: Automobile insurance.

Practical step: Ask what a property settlement or release covers before signing. Do not assume it resolves only repairs or automatically includes the injury claim.

Other claims require a separate review

A serious collision may raise additional issues, including a spouse’s or partner’s potential claim, work-related benefits, or claims following a death. Eligibility, parties, proof, and available damages differ. Tell the lawyer about these circumstances rather than treating them as extra items automatically added to your injury compensation.

Punitive damages are also different. They address qualifying misconduct and punishment, rather than simply reimbursing losses. They require clear and convincing proof of malice, oppression, or fraud; ordinary negligence or a serious injury alone does not establish entitlement. Corporate claims involve additional requirements. Judicial Council: CACI 3940, punitive damages.

What can limit or affect recovery?

Documenting losses is one part of the analysis. Other considerations include:

  • Responsibility: The evidence must support the legal claim and connect the conduct to the harm.
  • Your share of fault: Comparative fault may reduce damages according to your responsibility.
  • Coverage and payment sources: Insurance terms, limits, and collectibility can affect the practical outcome.
  • Legal restrictions: Some claims have restrictions on particular damages or different procedures.
  • Overlapping losses: The same harm should not be compensated twice under different labels.

Comparative fault requires an evidence-based evaluation; an insurer's allegation is not itself the final determination. Judicial Council: CACI 405, comparative fault.

An earlier condition also needs careful review. Share prior injuries and treatment so the accident-related changes can be distinguished. Medical-bill totals, injury labels, and online multipliers cannot answer all of these questions.

If you lacked insurance, tell the lawyer. Restrictions on noneconomic recovery can apply in certain motor-vehicle claims, but actual coverage, your role, and exceptions need review. Civil Code section 3333.4 (California Legislative Information).

Total recovery and the amount you receive

The gross settlement or recovery may differ from the money distributed to you.

Before accepting an offer, ask for an understandable explanation of attorney fees, case expenses, applicable medical bills or reimbursement claims, and your estimated net recovery. Ask which amounts are confirmed and what remains unresolved.

The written fee agreement should explain the percentage and how expenses affect the calculation. State Bar of California: Fees and billing.

Medi-Cal and Medicare may seek reimbursement for qualifying injury-related payments from a recovery. Private insurance or provider obligations may also need individual review. DHCS Personal Injury Program, Medicare conditional-payment information.

MMG’s fee policy: Contingency rates vary by case stage. MMG advances case expenses without an upfront payment. With no recovery, you owe MMG no attorney fees or case expenses. Medical bills and other third-party obligations are separate.

Organize your losses before the consultation

Use the printable loss-record worksheet to identify what you have and what is missing. Keep original documents and avoid sending sensitive medical information through an ordinary public contact form.

  • Medical providers, treatment dates, bills, and payment records.
  • Missed work, employment details, and medical restrictions.
  • Future-care recommendations and lasting limitations.
  • Household tasks affected and help received.
  • Meaningful changes in daily activities.
  • Damaged property, estimates, receipts, and transportation records.
  • Insurance documents, offers, notices, and any stated response dates.

You do not need to assign a dollar amount to every item before contacting MMG. Bring the facts and questions you already have.

Common questions about accident compensation

Can I claim future losses if I am still receiving treatment?

Potential future losses can be evaluated while treatment continues, but they require support. Ask what evidence is available now, what remains uncertain, and whether an offer accounts for those needs.

Are medical bills always paid in full by a settlement?

No. Recoverable medical expenses, available compensation, and your obligations to providers are separate issues. Ask how each will be handled.

Can pain and suffering be calculated by multiplying my bills?

There is no universal California multiplier that determines your entitlement. Evidence, applicable law, and individual circumstances matter.

Does free help from my family mean there is nothing to document?

No. Record the household tasks or care affected and the help provided. A lawyer can review its relevance and avoid overlapping categories.

What if I have not received an accident report yet?

You can still ask for an evaluation. Bring the date, location, report number if known, and available records. Missing documents can be identified during the discussion.

CALIFORNIA MOTORCYCLE CLAIMS

Motorcycle Damage, Riding Gear, and Property Claims in California

Document the loss. Understand your next step.

In this guide

Your bike is only part of the loss.

Document damaged equipment, keep cost records, and review the proposed settlement carefully.

01

Is the motorcycle in storage?

Confirm daily charges, inspection plans, and release requirements.

02

What needs to be documented?

Photograph the bike, riding gear, and personal belongings.

Your bike is only part of the loss

A motorcycle crash can damage the bike, helmet, protective clothing, luggage, and personal belongings. Towing and daily storage charges can arrive before an insurer decides fault. Start by documenting each loss and confirming where the motorcycle is being held.

If you were also injured, MMG can discuss how property issues fit alongside your injury claim. Call (818) 539-7969 or request a free case evaluation. Ask what assistance is available for your circumstances; standalone property-damage representation and its scope are not automatic.

Your next step

Bring the records you have.

Ask what property-claim assistance is available for your case.

Scope and fees are explained before representation. Third-party charges are separate.

Useful references

California insurance guidanceRepair complaint assistance

Keep the evidence. Track the costs.

Preserve photos, estimates, receipts, and insurance letters.

Start here if the motorcycle is in storage

  • Find the motorcycle’s exact location and the contact person who can authorize access or release.
  • Request an itemized bill, daily storage rate, current balance, release requirements, and any approaching lien-sale or disposal notice.
  • Notify the insurer promptly. Ask when inspection will occur, what charges it accepts, and whether moving the bike to a lower-cost location is appropriate.
  • Coordinate any necessary evidence inspection before repair, dismantling, or salvage transfer where possible. Keep written confirmation of arrangements.
  • Save every invoice and message. Record the date, person contacted, and response when a transfer or inspection is delayed.

Storage charges can continue during a dispute. Do not assume the insurer will pay every day indefinitely or that preserving evidence requires leaving the bike in an expensive yard. Discuss a reasonable plan that addresses both evidence and accumulating costs. If injuries prevent you from managing this, ask a trusted person to help with communications and confirm what authorization is required.

Build an inventory of the damaged property

Motorcycle and installed accessories

Record the year, make, model, VIN, mileage, pre-crash condition, and known prior damage. Photograph the entire bike and individual damage areas. List installed accessories separately, with receipts and installation records when available. Purchase price does not necessarily equal current value, and accessory spending may not increase a settlement dollar for dollar.

Helmet, jacket, boots, gloves, and protective equipment

Identify each item by brand, model, approximate purchase date, price, and pre-crash condition. Photograph damage, labels, and identifying information. Keep damaged gear available for inspection rather than discarding it immediately.

Preservation is not permission to reuse damaged safety equipment. Follow manufacturer guidance for a helmet involved in an impact; do not assume it is safe because the shell looks intact. For replacement selection, NHTSA’s motorcycle helmet guide explains fit and compliance labeling. A DOT marking reflects manufacturer certification, not individual NHTSA approval.

Luggage and personal items

Include damaged bags, communications equipment, phones, eyewear, and other belongings, explaining where they were and how the crash damaged them. Save receipts, account purchase histories, earlier photographs, and repair estimates. A missing receipt does not mean there is no other evidence of ownership or value.

Do not assume the motorcycle policy treats riding gear, permanently installed accessories, and personal belongings the same way. Ask which coverage and valuation method the insurer is applying to each item.

Repair estimate or total-loss offer?

The California Department of Insurance accident guide discusses vehicle damage estimates, actual cash value, and total-loss settlements. Request the insurer’s written estimate or valuation and its explanation of deductions. A loan balance is not the same as the motorcycle’s pre-loss value.

If repairs are proposed

Obtain an itemized estimate from a qualified motorcycle repairer. Ask what inspections support it, whether hidden damage may require a supplement, and what parts and labor are included. Clarify diagnostic, teardown, reassembly, and storage charges before authorizing work. An insurance estimate and your authorization to the shop are different documents.

The Bureau of Automotive Repair’s consumer guide explains written estimates, repair authorization, and invoices. Keep copies of the work approved and any later changes. A motorcycle should not be returned to service merely because cosmetic damage has been repaired; address safety concerns with the repair professional.

If the motorcycle is declared a total loss

Review whether the report identifies the correct model, mileage, equipment, condition, and relevant comparable motorcycles. Point out specific errors and provide dated supporting records. Ask for an explanation of applicable taxes and fees, deductions, and any salvage-retention amount.

Before retaining a totaled bike, clarify the payment adjustment, lender requirements, title and registration consequences, repair feasibility, and future insurability. Keeping the motorcycle does not establish that it is safe or legal to ride. If financing exceeds the settlement, check whether a separate gap agreement applies; it is not automatic protection.

Which insurance may help?

Your own collision coverage, if applicable, may address crash damage subject to a deductible and policy terms. A claim against a responsible party’s insurer depends on liability, covered damages, and available limits. Gear or accessory coverage may have separate terms. The California Department of Insurance coverage guide explains why the declarations and policy wording matter.

Ask which claim is being processed, whether a deductible applies, and how any later recovery from another party will be handled. Do not assume deductible reimbursement is guaranteed or immediate. Bodily-injury coverage and property-damage coverage are separate; identifying one does not establish the other.

Towing, transportation, and loss of use

Keep itemized towing, recovery, storage, and transport receipts. Reasonableness, necessity, causation, policy terms, and the type of claim can affect what is payable. Request written clarification rather than relying on a general statement that expenses are “covered.”

Rental reimbursement under your own policy is different from a potential loss-of-use claim against a responsible party. Ask about applicable limits and the period being considered before spending money you cannot afford to carry. Keep records of substitute transportation, dates the bike was unavailable, and repair or replacement delays. Do not assume that a rental motorcycle, every rideshare trip, or unlimited replacement time will be reimbursed.

Protect the injury claim when resolving property damage

A property settlement may be addressed before an injury claim is ready, but the actual release language matters. Confirm whether the document resolves only identified property losses or also releases bodily-injury claims, other parties, or unknown claims. Do not rely solely on a file label or an adjuster’s verbal description.

The bike and damaged gear may also be evidence of how the crash occurred. Coordinate preservation before signing salvage paperwork or authorizing disposal. Related guidance: motorcycle accident representation, compensation available after an accident, and insurance settlement offers and releases.

Where to seek assistance

For an insurer dispute, first request the decision and supporting explanation in writing. The California Department of Insurance provides consumer assistance for claim-handling concerns. A complaint does not guarantee payment or replace a lawsuit deadline.

For a repair transaction you cannot resolve with the shop, BAR’s complaint process may help evaluate or mediate an issue within its authority. Keep estimates, authorizations, invoices, and correspondence. This is assistance with qualifying repair disputes, not a promise of free repairs or cash reimbursement.

For a property-only dispute, the California Courts property-damage guide explains civil claims and potential small-claims options. Property-damage lawsuits generally have a three-year deadline, while injury lawsuits generally have a different, shorter period. Public-entity claims and other circumstances can require earlier action. Read MMG’s claim deadlines guide and obtain advice about your actual dates.

Bring the records you already have

For a consultation, useful starting materials include the crash date, motorcycle location, storage bill, claim number, photographs, repair estimate or total-loss offer, damaged-item list, and any proposed release. Tell MMG immediately if a storage deadline or salvage transfer is approaching.

MMG can discuss available assistance and the scope of any proposed representation. For accepted contingency injury matters, rates vary by case stage and are explained in the written agreement. Do not assume a property-only matter is accepted or handled without a fee. See attorney fees and case costs.

You were the passenger. Your injuries deserve their own review.

After a motorcycle crash, you may be facing treatment bills, missed work, and uncertainty about whose insurance should respond. You may also worry about making a claim when the operator is a friend, partner, or family member. Your options depend on what caused the crash, who may be legally responsible, and what coverage applies—not simply whose motorcycle you were riding.

Who may be responsible for a passenger’s injuries?

Another driver

A driver who turns across the motorcycle’s path, changes lanes unsafely, follows too closely, or otherwise drives negligently may be responsible if that conduct causes your injuries. The Judicial Council’s CACI 700 instruction explains drivers’ basic duty to use reasonable care, maintain a lookout, and control their vehicles.

The motorcycle operator

The person carrying you may also bear responsibility if their negligent operation caused or contributed to the crash. Riding with someone you know does not, by itself, eliminate a potential claim. A crash alone does not prove operator negligence; the movements, conditions, and available evidence need review.

More than one party

Both the operator and another driver may have contributed. Other circumstances may justify investigating a vehicle owner, an employer, a repair business, a defective component, or a dangerous roadway condition. Each theory requires its own facts and legal basis. Ownership, employment, or involvement alone does not establish liability.

You do not have to pick one version of events while injured and still gathering information. Preserve what you know and identify what you did not see.

If the operator is someone close to you

It is understandable to want medical expenses addressed without harming a relationship. A consultation can explain potential claims, applicable insurance, and the decisions involved before you choose how to proceed.

An insurance claim may be resolved without a lawsuit, but that cannot be promised. Nor can anyone promise that the operator will face no personal exposure, premium consequences, or other effects. Coverage and available limits must be checked rather than assumed.

Your interests and the operator’s interests may differ, especially when fault is disputed or insurance funds are limited. A lawyer must evaluate conflicts before representing both people. A shared ride does not necessarily mean shared representation is appropriate.

Which insurance may respond?

The California Department of Insurance consumer guide explains liability, uninsured/underinsured motorist, and medical-payments coverage. These are different types of protection. The guide provides background; it does not establish that a particular motorcycle passenger is covered.

  • Liability coverage: Review policies that may insure a legally responsible driver or operator. Who is insured, exclusions, and limits matter.
  • Uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage: Potential coverage under the motorcycle policy or another qualifying policy requires review of insured status, policy terms, statutory requirements, and any coverage rejection. It is not automatic.
  • Medical-payments coverage: If purchased and applicable, it may help with covered medical expenses without deciding fault, subject to its terms and limits.
  • Health coverage: It may help pay for treatment, but deductibles and potential reimbursement claims need separate attention.

Obtain declaration pages, policy information, and insurer letters where available. When multiple people are injured, a per-accident limit may be shared; do not assume each person can recover the full listed limit. Multiple policies also do not mean their limits can simply be added together.

Before accepting a settlement or signing a release, understand which parties and claims it covers and whether it could affect remaining insurance options. Related guides: uninsured and underinsured motorist claims and medical bills, liens, and treatment costs.

Evidence to preserve promptly

  • Names and contact details for the operator, other drivers, and independent witnesses.
  • Police report information and original photographs or video from before and after the crash.
  • Insurance cards, policy details, claim numbers, and correspondence.
  • Photographs of the motorcycle, passenger seat, footrests, helmet, and other damaged equipment.
  • Medical records, treatment instructions, bills, receipts, and work restrictions.
  • Your own factual account of seating position, what you observed, and what happened next.

Keep originals and backups. Do not fill gaps in memory with guesses or adopt someone else’s account as your own. Discuss inspection needs before disposal or repair of important equipment where possible, while addressing storage and insurer requirements promptly. Nearby video may be overwritten; a request does not guarantee footage exists or will be provided.

Passenger safety and disputed fault

Being a passenger does not automatically make you responsible for the operator’s driving. However, your own conduct may be examined. CACI 711 explains that passengers may generally expect reasonable care from a driver, but must take reasonable steps for their own safety when they become aware of danger or impaired or careless driving. What was known and reasonably possible matters.

California Vehicle Code section 27800 addresses passenger seating and footrests. Section 27803 requires compliant safety helmets for motorcycle operators and passengers. Equipment and helmet questions should be evaluated with the actual circumstances and injury evidence.

A missing helmet does not automatically resolve every aspect of a claim. The legal effect depends on the applicable rules and evidence connecting the conduct to the injuries at issue. Do not assume that an allegation ends your case. See partial fault in a California accident.

Document the effect on your life

Depending on the evidence and applicable law, a passenger’s claim may include medical expenses, lost earnings, reduced earning capacity, future care, and pain and suffering. Preserve information about limitations in work, mobility, sleep, household activities, and independence.

Report symptoms accurately to treating professionals and follow their advice. Future losses require supporting evidence; neither the seriousness of a crash nor a website calculator establishes their value. See compensation available after an accident and catastrophic injury representation.

KEEP ORIGINAL RECORDINGS, PHOTOGRAPHS, AND TREATMENT RECORDS.

What California requires before a lane change

Vehicle Code section 21658 addresses marked lanes: vehicles generally must remain within a single lane and must not leave it until the movement can be made with reasonable safety. Section 22107 separately addresses turning or moving right or left: the movement must be reasonably safe, and an appropriate signal is required when another vehicle may be affected.

A signal communicates an intention; it does not make an occupied space safe to enter. These duties apply to motorcycle riders as well as other drivers. Responsibility depends on the conduct that caused the collision, not simply which vehicle is larger or which person received a citation.

The California DMV’s lane-change guidance tells drivers to signal, examine mirrors and surrounding traffic, check over the shoulder, and ensure sufficient space. Its instructions specifically call for checking blind spots for motorcycles. These practical precautions help frame the investigation; they do not replace an assessment of the particular facts.

Three conflicts that need different evidence

A driver moves into a rider’s occupied lane

The investigation should establish the motorcycle’s position before the vehicle crossed the line. Relevant details include turn-signal timing, traffic speed, lateral movement, and what the driver could have observed. Contact damage may help test the accounts, but damage alone may not reconstruct the whole event.

Two vehicles move toward the same gap

When both vehicles are changing lanes, the first task is to establish their paths and timing. Which lane did each start in? Was either already established in the destination lane? Could either person reasonably recognize and respond to the other’s movement? Avoid assuming that the person who signaled first automatically had priority.

A merge, lane ending, or last-minute exit creates a conflict

Preserve the signs, taper, lane markings, and road configuration. An entrance ramp, ending travel lane, construction diversion, and driveway entry can raise different questions. The analysis should identify the actual maneuver rather than apply a blanket “merging vehicle always loses” rule.

A blind-spot explanation is a starting point

“I never saw the motorcycle” does not resolve whether the driver used reasonable care. The DMV’s motorcycle-sharing guidance explains that motorcycles are smaller and can disappear in vehicle blind spots, and tells drivers to check for them when changing lanes or entering a road.

Useful questions include the vehicle’s size and mirror arrangement, the motorcycle’s position over time, visibility obstructions, and whether the driver checked before moving. A later photograph may show the roadway without reproducing the traffic or lighting at the time of the crash. Label when it was taken.

A blind-spot monitor also does not settle the issue. Do not assume the vehicle had one, that it would detect every motorcycle, or that it retained useful records. Equipment, operating conditions, and available data must be identified before drawing conclusions.

Evidence to preserve promptly

  • Original video: Keep helmet-camera, dashcam, and other recordings, including the approach and aftermath. Back up originals; do not edit the only copy.
  • Independent witnesses: Save contact information and each witness’s viewing position. Someone behind the vehicles may have seen lane movement that another witness missed.
  • Roadway photographs: When safe, document lane boundaries, merging signs, obstructions, construction, debris, and final vehicle positions.
  • Damage and equipment: Photograph both sides of the motorcycle and damaged riding equipment. Discuss inspection needs before repair, disposal, or salvage transfer where possible; address storage requirements promptly.
  • Reports and communications: Keep the incident number, report, insurer correspondence, and a factual account of what you remember. Separate personal observations from information learned afterward.
  • Injury and income records: Save treatment instructions, bills, receipts, work restrictions, missed-work documentation, and notes about daily limitations.

Nearby recordings may be overwritten quickly. A preservation request should identify the date, location, time period, and material sought, but it does not guarantee that footage exists or will be provided voluntarily. Not every traffic camera records. Electronic vehicle data may help in some cases, but availability varies and it may not establish a lane change by itself.

What if the rider was lane splitting or partly at fault?

Lane splitting and changing from one lane to another are different movements. Identify what the rider was actually doing before deciding which issues apply. Allegations about speed, lane position, or visibility should be tested against evidence and their connection to the crash. See California lane-splitting accidents for that separate discussion.

California comparative fault can allow recovery even when an injured person shares responsibility, with damages reduced according to that person’s percentage of fault. The Judicial Council’s CACI 405 instruction explains this allocation.

For illustration only: $100,000 in proven damages reduced by 20% rider fault equals $80,000 before attorney fees, expenses, liens, and other applicable deductions. This calculation does not predict case value, insurance coverage, or actual payment. Read partial fault in a California accident.

Injury evidence and potential compensation

Documenting an unsafe movement is only part of a claim. Medical and other evidence must also connect the collision to the injuries and losses claimed. Depending on the facts and applicable law, compensation may include medical expenses, lost income, diminished earning capacity, future care, pain and suffering, and property damage.

Report symptoms accurately to treating professionals and follow their advice. Keep track of changes in mobility, sleep, work, and ordinary activities without guessing at diagnoses or future costs. Lasting limitations may require medical opinions and additional documentation.

A driver turned across your path. What happens next?

An approaching car turns left. You brake, swerve, or strike its side. Afterward, the driver says they never saw you—and the insurer starts asking about your speed. A left-turn motorcycle claim should examine the movements of both vehicles, the available sight lines, and the evidence of your injuries.

If the collision just happened, move out of traffic if you can do so safely, call 911 when emergency help is needed, and seek appropriate medical care. Do not put yourself at risk to photograph the scene.

Four questions that help clarify disputed fault

  • Where was the motorcycle when the driver began turning?
  • What could each person see, including around stopped vehicles and other obstructions?
  • Which signals, signs, and lane markings governed their movements?
  • What do independent evidence and witness accounts establish about timing, speed, and opportunities to avoid the crash?

The point of impact is one piece of the sequence. A motorcycle hitting the side of a car does not, by itself, establish who had the right of way.

California right of way depends on the sequence

Under California Vehicle Code section 21801, a driver turning left must yield to approaching traffic close enough to create a hazard during the turn and wait until the movement can be made reasonably safely. The statute also addresses what happens after the driver properly yields and signals: approaching drivers must then yield to that turning movement. A left turn alone does not decide liability.

The Judicial Council’s CACI 704 left-turn instruction focuses on whether a reasonably careful person would recognize the danger of a collision. When a turn crosses multiple lanes, hazards in each oncoming lane matter. One driver stopping or waving someone through does not establish that the motorcycle’s lane is clear.

Traffic controls also matter. A protected arrow, a permissive turn, a changing signal, or a driveway entrance can present different factual questions. The investigation should identify the actual control and sequence rather than assume that every intersection follows the same pattern.

Visibility deserves evidence, not assumptions

“I didn’t see the motorcycle” describes a driver’s account; it does not settle whether the driver acted reasonably. The California DMV’s sharing-the-road guidance explains that motorcycles can be harder to see and can disappear in blind spots.

Useful questions include whether a larger vehicle blocked the view, whether the driver looked again before crossing the next lane, and whether lighting or road geometry affected the sight line. Photographs taken later should be identified as later photographs: different traffic, sunlight, parked vehicles, or construction may change what they show.

A rider’s position, headlight condition, clothing, and movements may be investigated when relevant. Those facts require context. Neither a visibility allegation nor a statement that the rider “came out of nowhere” substitutes for reconstructing the approach.

Evidence to preserve promptly

  • Original video: Save dashcam, helmet-camera, or other recordings in their original form, with footage from before and after the collision. Keep a backup; avoid editing the only copy.
  • Witness information: Preserve names, contact details, and what each person actually observed, including their location and direction of travel.
  • Scene details: Keep safe photographs of lane markings, signs, sight obstructions, debris, vehicle positions, and road conditions. Label the date and source.
  • Motorcycle and riding equipment: Photograph damage and discuss inspection needs before repair, disposal, or salvage transfer when possible. Coordinate storage and insurer requirements promptly.
  • Reports and communications: Keep the incident number, report, insurer letters, messages, and your own factual timeline. Distinguish what you remember from what others later told you.
  • Medical and work records: Preserve treatment records, discharge instructions, receipts, restrictions, missed-work records, and notes about changes in daily activities.

Nearby businesses or homes may have useful recordings, but some systems overwrite quickly. Traffic cameras do not necessarily record or retain video. Signal timing plans may help explain operation without proving which light a particular driver faced at the exact moment. Requests should identify the location, date, and relevant time period; access and retention vary.

What if the insurer blames the rider?

California uses comparative fault. A person who shares responsibility may still recover damages, with compensation reduced by the percentage of fault assigned to that person. The Judicial Council’s CACI 405 comparative-fault instruction explains this allocation.

For illustration only, if proven damages were $100,000 and the rider were assigned 20% responsibility, the resulting amount would be $80,000 before attorney fees, expenses, liens, and other applicable deductions. This is arithmetic, not a prediction of case value or available insurance.

Speed, lane changes, and lane splitting may become disputed issues. An allegation needs supporting evidence and a connection to the collision. Read MMG’s related guides to partial fault in a California accident and California lane-splitting accidents.

Injuries and future needs are part of the claim

Liability evidence explains how the crash happened. Medical evidence helps establish which injuries it caused and how those injuries affect your life. Depending on the evidence and applicable law, a claim may include medical expenses, lost earnings, reduced earning capacity, future care, pain and suffering, and property damage.

Describe symptoms accurately to treating professionals and follow their advice. Keep records of limitations such as difficulty standing, returning to work, driving, sleeping, or performing household tasks. Future losses require support; they should not be guessed from an injury label or a website calculator.
