What California law and guidance say

The California Highway Patrol’s lane-splitting guidance confirms that lane splitting is legal in California and reproduces Vehicle Code section 21658.1. The definition addresses motorcycles with two wheels on the ground traveling between rows of stopped or moving vehicles. It includes divided and undivided roads.

The section authorizes educational guidance; it does not establish a universal numerical lane-splitting speed allowance. Do not treat a claimed “10 mph rule” or “30 mph rule” as permission to disregard conditions or other traffic laws.

CHP explains that risk increases with overall speed and the speed difference between the motorcycle and surrounding traffic. It also distinguishes lane splitting from riding on the shoulder, which it identifies as illegal. CHP states that intentionally blocking a rider in a way that could cause harm, or opening a door to impede a rider, is illegal.

These points are not a formula for deciding every claim. The location, movements, traffic controls, and conduct of the people involved require individual review.

Four questions that help clarify disputed fault

Where were the motorcycle and other vehicle?

Document the lanes, lane markings, traffic direction, and position of each vehicle before contact. A description such as “the motorcycle came out of nowhere” does not establish the rider’s actual position or visibility. Video and physical evidence may support or contradict that description.

Travel between rows of traffic, shoulder travel, a turn, and crossing into another lane can raise different questions. Use the actual route and roadway markings rather than relying only on the label “lane splitting.”

What changed immediately before the collision?

A lane change, merge, turn, opened door, narrowing gap, or sudden traffic movement may be important. Investigators may need to determine whether a signal was used, when movement began, and how much time was available to respond.

The California DMV’s guidance on sharing the road reminds drivers to check blind spots before turning or changing lanes and recognizes legal lane sharing with motorcycles. A driver’s use of a signal is relevant evidence, but it does not alone establish that the movement was safe.

What do speed and visibility evidence show?

The motorcycle’s speed, traffic speed, sight lines, lighting, and available space may all matter. A witness’s estimate should be considered alongside where the witness was located and what they could observe.

Avoid drawing a firm speed conclusion from damage alone or from a short clip without context. Qualified reconstruction may help evaluate timing and movement when the available evidence supports it. An investigation should test the rider’s account and other accounts fairly.

Which conduct actually contributed to the injury?

The claim must connect relevant conduct to the collision or injury. The question is not simply whether someone dislikes lane splitting or whether one person received a citation. A police report, insurer assessment, and witness statement are pieces of evidence, rather than substitutes for the complete analysis.

Read Motorcycle Accident Lawyer for the broader claim process and Multi-Vehicle Accident Lawyer when several vehicles were involved.

What if the rider is partly responsible?

California’s comparative-fault principles may permit recovery even when an injured person contributed to the harm, with damages reduced according to their share of responsibility. The Judicial Council’s CACI 405 instruction, reproduced by Justia, explains the reduction when a defendant proves the injured person’s negligent conduct was a substantial factor in causing the harm.

For illustration only, if recoverable damages were $100,000 and the injured rider were assigned 20% of the responsibility, a simple comparative-fault reduction would leave $80,000 before fees, costs, liens, and any other applicable adjustments. This is not a case valuation or a prediction about your claim.

An insurer’s proposed percentage is not necessarily the final answer. Ask what facts support it and what evidence may be missing. See Partial Fault in a California Accident and Insurance Settlement Offers and Releases.

Evidence to preserve promptly

  • Original camera footage: save helmet-camera, motorcycle-camera, and dash-camera files, including footage before and after the event. Keep the original recording rather than only a social-media clip.
  • Witness details: preserve names, contact information, and where each witness was located. Separate firsthand observations from later opinions.
  • Roadway photographs: lane markings, traffic controls, road width, lighting, and the location of debris may help explain the setting. Do not return to an unsafe location to take photos.
  • Motorcycle and vehicle damage: photographs and appropriately coordinated inspections may help assess the contact sequence. Tell the attorney about planned repairs or disposal.
  • Helmet and riding gear: retain damaged items when possible and discuss preservation. Do not reuse crash-damaged protective equipment merely to preserve a claim.
  • Reports and communications: save the report number, exchange information, insurer letters, and messages about how the crash occurred.
  • Treatment and financial records: preserve medical records, bills, missed-work information, and receipts for related expenses.

Camera footage may be overwritten. Identifying potential sources promptly can help, but a preservation request does not itself compel disclosure or authorize access to private devices or property. Your attorney can address appropriate requests and inspections.

Practical next steps after a lane-splitting crash

Prioritize safety and medical care. If you can do so safely, collect the other driver’s information and witness contacts. Write a short account while your memory is fresh: your direction, surrounding traffic, what changed, and where contact occurred.

Describe what you observed without filling gaps through guesses. Share relevant facts with your attorney, including anything you think may be unfavorable. Do not delete or alter recordings because a portion seems unhelpful.

Have deadlines reviewed promptly. The California Courts’ deadline guidance explains that filing limits depend on the claim and circumstances. Negotiations do not automatically extend them. Read California Accident Claim Deadlines.

Document the effects of the injury

The claim should address actual injuries and losses, not stereotypes about riders. Follow treating clinicians’ instructions and keep a record of treatment, missed work, and help needed at home. Long-term losses require appropriate medical and financial support.

Depending on the facts and law, recoverable damages may include medical expenses, lost income, future losses, and pain and suffering. No amount can be promised because the collision involved lane splitting. See Compensation Available After an Accident, Traumatic Brain Injury, and Catastrophic Injury Lawyer.

COMMON QUESTIONS

Common questions about lane-splitting claims

The legality of lane splitting makes that label alone an incomplete fault analysis. An insurer may dispute other facts, coverage, or causation. Preserve the denial and its stated reasons so they can be evaluated.

No single number resolves all conditions or legal duties. Section 21658.1 does not create a blanket numerical safe harbor. Speed, visibility, traffic movements, roadway rules, and the particular maneuver still matter.

Preserve video, witnesses, and any relevant statements. An allegation of deliberate conduct needs evidence, and it may raise distinct claim and insurance questions. Avoid confronting the driver; discuss the available facts with the attorney.

A claim may still warrant review if another vehicle’s movement led to a fall or evasive maneuver. Proving that sequence can be difficult, and insurance coverage may have separate requirements. Promptly preserve video and witnesses.

Understand why the truck overturned—and what comes next

A truck rollover can leave nearby drivers facing an overturned trailer, spilled cargo, or a sudden chain of collisions. For someone injured, the immediate concerns are medical care, disrupted work, and how to get reliable answers.

A rollover describes what happened to the truck. It does not, by itself, establish why it happened or who is responsible. An investigation should connect the truck’s movement to its speed, load, road conditions, equipment, and any other vehicles involved.

FMCSA cargo tank guidanceFederal stability-control standard

Preserve evidence before it changes.

Video, loading records, and inspections can help establish the sequence.

How a rollover can develop

A truck rolls over when it tips onto its side or roof. Investigators may examine a turn or abrupt maneuver, a departure from the roadway, contact with a curb or uneven ground, or an impact with another vehicle. The order matters: a collision can precede the rollover, or the overturning truck can cause subsequent impacts.

A jackknife is a different movement, involving a tractor and trailer folding toward each other. A crash may involve both, but the terms should not replace a reconstruction of the sequence. See Jackknife Truck Accidents.

FMCSA’s cargo tank rollover prevention resource considers vehicle design, load effects, highway factors, and driver factors. Its training is specifically directed at cargo tank operations. It provides useful context, but findings about tank trucks should not be treated as proof about every tractor-trailer or individual crash.

Four questions that guide the investigation

Was speed appropriate for the situation?

An investigation should examine speed approaching a curve, ramp, lane change, or unexpected hazard—not simply the posted speed limit. Load characteristics, the roadway, and the maneuver may affect the analysis. Video, available electronic records, physical evidence, and qualified reconstruction may help assess speed and timing.

A photograph of the overturned truck cannot establish its earlier speed. Nor does a rollover automatically prove that the driver was speeding. Competing explanations should be tested against the evidence.

What was loaded, and how was it distributed?

The height and distribution of a load can affect stability. Relevant questions may include the type of cargo, loading arrangement, weight, securement, and whether material moved before or during the crash. Liquid cargo raises different questions from pallets, machinery, or loose materials.

For covered cargo, 49 CFR 393.100 addresses preventing cargo from escaping and preventing movement that adversely affects vehicle stability or maneuverability. Investigators should evaluate the actual loading system and applicable requirements.

Cargo scattered after a rollover does not alone establish that improper loading caused it. Loading documents, photographs taken before departure, and physical examination may help distinguish cause from consequence. Read Overloaded Trucks and Unsecured Cargo.

What role did the road and weather play?

Curve geometry, pavement condition, shoulder drop-offs, traction, visibility, and wind may warrant examination. Conditions at the precise location and time matter. A general weather report or photograph taken days later may not capture what the driver encountered.

For covered operations, 49 CFR 392.14 requires extreme caution when hazardous conditions affect traction or visibility, reduced speed, and discontinuing operation when conditions become sufficiently dangerous, subject to the rule’s limited exception. Weather is part of the investigation, not an automatic answer to responsibility.

If a roadway condition may be involved, identifying the responsible entity and reviewing any special claim requirements promptly can be important. See California Accident Claim Deadlines.

What do the vehicle and stability systems show?

Depending on the truck and circumstances, inspection may address tires, suspension, brakes, steering, coupling components, and electronic stability equipment. 49 CFR 396.3 addresses systematic inspection, repair, and maintenance for covered vehicles. An identified defect must still be connected to the crash or resulting harm.

Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 136 addresses electronic stability control for covered heavy vehicles. Vehicle category, manufacturing date, and exceptions matter. The standard should not be described as requiring the same equipment on every commercial truck.

The presence of stability control does not mean that every rollover can be prevented. A rollover likewise does not establish that the system failed. Investigators may need to identify the installed equipment, available diagnostic or event records, warning history, and performance under the actual conditions. Related guidance: Truck Brake Failure and Poor Maintenance.

Evidence to preserve before it changes

  • Truck, trailer, and relevant components: qualified inspections may help assess damage, condition, and the relationship between equipment and the crash.
  • Original video and photographs: footage before the rollover can be especially useful. Preserve original files and identify nearby cameras promptly.
  • Scene evidence: road measurements, tire marks, debris, shoulder conditions, and vehicle resting positions may help establish movement and timing.
  • Loading and weight records: shipping documents, loading photographs, weight tickets, and available instructions may clarify the load before the event.
  • Vehicle and trip data: available telematics, event records, dispatch messages, and duty-status logs may help answer different questions. Not every system records the same information.
  • Inspection and maintenance history: records may reveal earlier concerns, repairs, component changes, or diagnostic warnings.
  • Witness information: record where each witness was located and what they observed before, during, and after the rollover.

Repairs, salvage, cleanup, and routine overwriting may change or remove evidence. Tell the attorney where the vehicles are stored and whether disposal is planned, if you know. A preservation request identifies material to retain; it does not itself compel disclosure or authorize entry onto private property.

Do not inspect unstable vehicles, enter traffic, handle spilled cargo, or arrange testing yourself. Evidence collection should be coordinated safely and appropriately. Read Truck Accident Evidence Preservation.

Who may need to be investigated?

Potentially relevant parties may include the driver, motor carrier, equipment owner, loading business, maintenance provider, manufacturer, or another motorist. Roadway-related claims may raise additional requirements. The facts and applicable law determine which parties, if any, are responsible.

Company records can help identify who controlled the trip, supplied the equipment, performed repairs, or loaded the trailer. A company’s name on the truck does not resolve all business relationships or insurance questions. See Trucking Company Liability.

If several vehicles were involved, the investigation should distinguish the initial event from later impacts. Different insurers may advance conflicting explanations. Preserve correspondence and the information supporting each account. Read Multi-Vehicle Accident Lawyer.

Document injuries and long-term needs

Seek appropriate medical care and follow your clinicians’ instructions. Save treatment records, receipts, missed-work information, and records of assistance needed at home. Serious injuries may require documentation of rehabilitation, reduced earning capacity, and medically supported future care.

A claim should reflect the person’s actual losses and prognosis. The collision type alone cannot establish a case value. Related MMG guides explain Catastrophic Injuries, Spinal Cord Injury and Paralysis, and Compensation Available After an Accident.

What you can do now

Prioritize safety and medical needs. Save the crash report number, original photos and videos, witness details, and insurer communications. Make a short timeline while events are fresh, distinguishing what you saw from information received later.

Have deadlines reviewed promptly. The California Courts’ filing-deadline guidance explains that time limits depend on the claim and circumstances. Insurance discussions and evidence-preservation efforts do not automatically extend the time to file.

Common questions about truck rollover claims

No. The investigation should address the driver’s conduct, equipment, load, roadway, other vehicles, and causation. The truck’s final position alone does not decide responsibility.

Yes. The arrangement and movement of cargo may raise stability questions independently of total weight. Investigators need evidence of the actual load rather than assumptions based on the wreckage.

Identify the system and preserve available records. Its presence does not guarantee prevention of a particular crash, and the occurrence of a rollover does not establish a malfunction.

A claim may still require review if the rollover, spilled cargo, or evasive action led to your injury. Proving the sequence and evaluating coverage may be especially important. Save witnesses and original video where available.

A jackknife alone does not establish fault.

Understand the sequence—not just the final position

A jackknife occurs when a tractor and its attached trailer fold toward each other as the combination loses its normal alignment. The truck or trailer may swing across lanes, strike nearby vehicles, or leave other drivers facing a sudden obstruction.

The truck’s final position does not, by itself, explain why the crash happened or who was responsible. An investigation should establish what happened before the loss of control, how the vehicles moved, and when each impact occurred.

Useful references

California DMV truck guidanceFMCSA logging guidance

Preserve the evidence before it changes.

Video, vehicle records, and witness accounts may matter.

How a jackknife can develop

Tractor-trailers pivot at their coupling during normal turns. A jackknife involves an uncontrolled change in that relationship. Investigators may consider a loss of tire traction, braking behavior, steering inputs, road conditions, or contact with another vehicle. More than one factor may be involved.

The California DMV’s truck-driver guidance explains how braking problems and wheel lockups can affect control and contribute to jackknifing. This is useful safety context, but it does not establish the cause of a particular crash.

A trailer swinging outward, a tractor rotating, and a truck rolling over are not interchangeable descriptions. A crash can involve several movements. Video, physical evidence, and qualified reconstruction may help distinguish them and establish their order.

What investigators may need to examine

Speed, following distance, and braking

The important questions include the truck’s speed before the event, the space available to respond, and whether braking began before or after another impact. A damaged brake component may require examination to distinguish an earlier problem from crash damage. Investigators should not assume that every jackknife resulted from excessive speed or failed brakes.

Weather, pavement, and visibility

Rain, ice, debris, curves, grades, and reduced visibility may affect the analysis. Evidence should reflect conditions at the place and time of the crash, rather than a general weather report alone.

For covered commercial operations, 49 CFR 392.14 requires extreme caution when hazardous conditions affect traction or visibility, reduced speed, and discontinuing operation when conditions become sufficiently dangerous, subject to the rule’s limited exception. Bad weather therefore does not automatically resolve questions about the driver’s conduct. Applicability and the actual circumstances require review.

Equipment and maintenance

Brake systems, tires, steering, and relevant stability-control equipment may warrant inspection. 49 CFR 396.3 addresses systematic inspection, repair, and maintenance for covered vehicles. The investigation should connect any identified condition to the loss of control, rather than assume a maintenance violation caused the crash.

Read Truck Brake Failure and Poor Maintenance for related evidence questions.

Cargo and other vehicles

Loading records and the condition of the load may help assess whether weight distribution or cargo movement played a role. Federal cargo securement requirements address preventing cargo from escaping and preventing shifting that adversely affects stability or maneuverability. Displaced cargo found after an impact does not alone establish that it caused the jackknife.

Another vehicle’s lane change, collision, or sudden movement may also be relevant. A complete reconstruction should test competing explanations. See Overloaded Trucks and Unsecured Cargo.

Evidence that can clarify the crash sequence

  • Original video: dash cameras, nearby businesses, and other vehicles may show movement before the truck reached its final position. Save original files, not only edited clips.
  • Scene photographs and measurements: tire marks, debris, vehicle positions, road geometry, and damage can help connect separate events.
  • Electronic vehicle data: available engine, braking, stability-control, or telematics records may provide useful information. The systems installed, recorded events, and data retention vary.
  • Driver and trip records: duty-status logs, dispatch communications, route information, and available delivery records may help establish the timeline.
  • Inspection and repair records: service history, reported concerns, replacement parts, and post-crash examinations may help distinguish old conditions from impact damage.
  • Loading documents: shipping records, weight information, and loading instructions may identify relevant cargo questions.
  • Witness accounts: where a witness was located and what they actually saw matter as much as the conclusion they reached.

An electronic logging device is not automatically a detailed crash recorder. Duty-status records and event data from other vehicle systems serve different purposes. An attorney or qualified expert can identify which records may exist and how to obtain them appropriately.

FMCSA’s ELD guidance states that motor carriers must retain ELD duty-status and backup data for six months. That does not mean every vehicle-data system or video source retains information for that long, or that waiting is advisable.

Repairs, salvage, and routine overwriting may affect evidence. A preservation request can identify relevant material, but it does not itself compel disclosure or authorize access to someone else’s vehicle. Inspections and testing should be coordinated appropriately. See Truck Accident Evidence Preservation.

Who may be responsible?

Depending on the facts, investigation may involve the driver, motor carrier, equipment owner, maintenance provider, loading business, manufacturer, or another motorist. Each potential claim needs a supported legal basis and a connection to the harm.

Company records may help establish who controlled the trip and equipment. A business name on a trailer does not answer every ownership, employment, or insurance question. Learn more about Trucking Company Liability.

In a chain-reaction collision, the sequence matters: a vehicle may strike the truck, be struck by it, or collide with a separate obstruction afterward. Multiple insurers may reach different conclusions. Keep their correspondence and avoid assuming one adjuster’s explanation resolves all claims. See Multi-Vehicle Accident Lawyer.

Document injuries and the effect on daily life

Seek appropriate medical care and follow the treating clinician’s instructions. Keep treatment records, receipts, missed-work information, and a simple record of assistance needed at home. Serious injuries may require documentation of rehabilitation, reduced earning capacity, and medically supported future care.

The claim should reflect the person’s actual condition and prognosis. Neither the label “jackknife” nor dramatic vehicle damage establishes a settlement amount. Related guides explain Catastrophic Injuries and Compensation Available After an Accident.

Practical next steps

  • Prioritize safety and medical care. Do not enter traffic or approach unstable equipment to gather evidence.
  • Save your original photos, videos, report number, witness details, and insurer letters.
  • Tell the attorney where the vehicles are stored and whether repairs, salvage, or disposal are planned, if you know.
  • Describe what you observed separately from what someone later told you.
  • Have filing deadlines reviewed promptly. Evidence retention periods and legal filing deadlines are different.

Read California Accident Claim Deadlines. An ongoing insurance investigation does not automatically extend the time to bring a claim.

No. The investigation must address the circumstances, applicable duties, and causation. Driver conduct, equipment, road conditions, and other vehicles may need review together.

Possibly. Evidence may connect a truck’s movement to a collision involving evasive action or another vehicle. Lack of contact can create proof and coverage questions, so preserve witnesses and video and have the facts reviewed.

An accusation does not settle the issue. California’s comparative-fault rules may allow recovery reduced by an injured person’s share of responsibility, depending on the claim and applicable law. See Partial Fault in a California Accident.

The report is one source of evidence. Witnesses, video, vehicle inspections, and other records may add information. Identify specific discrepancies rather than assuming the report is complete or entirely wrong.

Understand what happened—and what your family needs next

An underride collision occurs when a smaller vehicle travels partly beneath a truck or trailer. The height difference can expose the passenger compartment to forces it was not designed to absorb in the same way as an ordinary vehicle-to-vehicle impact.

After a serious crash, families may need answers about the collision, the truck’s protective equipment, and the care an injured person will require. An investigation should examine both what caused the crash and whether the vehicle’s condition or protective equipment contributed to the severity of the injuries.

Useful references

Federal rear-impact rulesGAO underride report

Preserve evidence before it changes.

Ask about vehicle storage, inspections, and original footage.

Rear and side underride involve different questions

Rear underride

A smaller vehicle may travel under the rear of a truck or trailer. Investigators may examine the collision sequence, visibility, braking, and the presence, condition, installation, and performance of rear-impact protection.

The fact that a passenger vehicle struck the rear does not answer every question about responsibility or enhanced injuries. Equally, the occurrence of underride does not by itself prove that a guard violated a standard or that a particular business is liable.

Side underride

A smaller vehicle may travel beneath the side of a trailer, including during a crossing or turning movement. Important evidence can include the vehicles’ paths, lighting, visibility, timing, and the trailer’s configuration.

Rear-impact standards should not be treated as side-impact standards. NHTSA’s 2024 report to Congress on side underride protection discusses research and rulemaking activity; that report itself is not a final requirement that every trailer have a side guard. The rules and legal duties applicable to a particular vehicle and crash date need individual review.

Why these crashes require careful investigation

Underride can involve intrusion into the occupant space and devastating injuries. The U.S. Government Accountability Office’s underride report discusses the risks of serious injury and death, as well as limitations in crash reporting and the need for better information about these events.

That research provides context, not a conclusion about an individual crash. A report’s label, a photograph, or a general statistic cannot replace examination of the actual vehicles and sequence.

Two questions may require different evidence: what caused the vehicles to collide, and what caused particular injuries during the collision. Qualified reconstruction and engineering analysis may help evaluate these issues alongside medical evidence. Conclusions must account for the impact conditions and alternative explanations.

Which rear-impact guard rules may apply?

Federal rules distinguish requirements for certain trailers and semitrailers from those for other covered vehicles. Manufacturing date, vehicle configuration, and exceptions matter. A single rule or measurement should not be presented as applying to every truck.

  • Motor-carrier requirements: 49 CFR 393.86 addresses rear-impact guards and rear-end protection, including different vehicle categories and exceptions.
  • Guard performance: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 223 addresses rear-impact guard requirements and testing.
  • Vehicle installation: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 224 addresses rear-impact protection on covered trailers and semitrailers, including configuration and installation requirements.

A guard’s presence does not alone establish compliance, adequate maintenance, or performance in the particular crash. Likewise, damage after impact does not alone establish a preexisting defect. The relevant standards and the condition of the equipment must be evaluated together.

Evidence to preserve promptly

Repairs, salvage, and disposal can change important evidence. An early investigation may identify the truck, trailer, passenger vehicle, guard, and related components that should be preserved through appropriate arrangements.

  • Both vehicles: damage patterns and the relationship between the vehicles may help reconstruct the impact.
  • Guard and attachments: photographs, measurements, mounting points, and available components may help assess installation, condition, and failure.
  • Vehicle identification and specifications: VINs, manufacturing information, guard identification, and relevant design documents help establish what equipment and standards are involved.
  • Inspection and repair history: records may reveal prior damage, repairs, alterations, or reported concerns.
  • Video and scene information: original dash-camera footage, nearby video, witness accounts, road layout, and lighting may help establish timing and visibility.
  • Trip and operational records: dispatch information and available vehicle data may provide context, depending on the systems actually used.
  • Medical and care records: treatment information helps document injuries, limitations, and evolving needs.

A preservation request does not itself authorize access to private property or compel production. Vehicle inspection and any testing that changes evidence should be coordinated appropriately. Do not remove guard components or arrange unauthorized testing yourself. Read Truck Accident Evidence Preservation.

Who may need to be investigated?

The driver, motor carrier, trailer owner, maintenance provider, and equipment manufacturer may have different roles. Relevant questions include who operated the trip, who controlled the equipment, what work was performed, and whether a supported defect or negligent act contributed to the harm.

A product-related claim may involve design, manufacturing, or installation issues. A maintenance-related claim may involve prior damage or repair decisions. These possibilities require evidence and a legal basis; naming a business connected to the truck is not enough.

For related guidance, see Trucking Company Liability and Truck Brake Failure and Poor Maintenance.

Document serious injuries and long-term needs

The claim should reflect the injured person’s actual condition, not assumptions based on how the crash looks. Treating clinicians determine diagnosis and treatment. Legal evaluation may require documentation of hospitalization, rehabilitation, missed work, assistance at home, and medically supported future needs.

Keep discharge instructions, appointment information, receipts, and a simple record of help provided by family members. Avoid treating an early estimate as a final picture when recovery and future needs remain uncertain.

Related MMG guides address Catastrophic Injury, Traumatic Brain Injury, and Spinal Cord Injury and Paralysis. Families who have lost someone can review Wrongful Death After a Vehicle Accident for information about seeking representation.

What you can do now

Prioritize medical care. Save original photos and video, the report number, witness details, and insurer correspondence. If you know where either vehicle is stored or whether repairs or disposal are planned, share that information promptly with the attorney.

You do not need to revisit an unsafe scene or inspect a truck yourself. If you are helping an injured relative, explain your relationship when contacting the firm; the attorney can address who has authority to act or obtain records.

Filing deadlines and evidence preservation are separate concerns. An insurer’s ongoing investigation does not automatically extend a deadline. See California Accident Claim Deadlines.

The inspection may be relevant, but investigators should examine what was inspected, when, and what happened afterward. A prior inspection does not alone establish the equipment’s condition during a later collision.

Tell the attorney what you know. Photographs, repair records, stored components, video, and other evidence may remain. Missing evidence does not automatically establish misconduct or mean that a claim cannot proceed.

Depending on the evidence and applicable law, a claim may address medical expenses, lost earnings, future care, and other recoverable losses. No amount can be promised from the collision type alone. See Compensation Available After an Accident.

IN THIS GUIDE

Three different cargo questions

Overloading

What did the vehicle and load weigh?

Shifting loads

Did movement affect vehicle control?

Falling cargo

When and where did the material fall?

Cargo on the road after impact does not prove it caused the crash.

When the load becomes part of the crash

Cargo can create danger without the truck striking another vehicle directly. A shifting load may affect control, falling freight can hit someone or obstruct traffic, and an improperly loaded truck may be involved in a rollover or a chain-reaction collision.

The key questions are what the truck carried, how it was loaded and secured, and whether a loading problem contributed to the crash. Cargo found on the road after impact does not, by itself, prove that it fell before the collision or caused it.

Useful references

FMCSA cargo securementCaltrans weight guidance

Preserve evidence before it changes.

Original photos, loading records, and witness accounts may matter.

Overloading, shifting loads, and falling cargo are different issues

Overloading: weight and vehicle limits

An investigation may examine total vehicle-and-load weight, axle loading, applicable limits, and any permit. A truck's appearance does not establish that it was overweight. Scale tickets, shipping records, vehicle specifications, and the actual load can provide a better foundation.

California weight rules involve more than a single statewide number. Axle configuration and spacing, the route, and applicable exceptions or permits may matter. Caltrans explains California truck weight limitations and oversize or overweight permits. A permit does not eliminate cargo-securement duties or establish that the truck was operated safely.

Shifting loads: distribution and movement

Cargo can move inside a trailer even if nothing falls onto the road. The investigation may consider load placement, restraint systems, the direction of movement, and how the truck was turning, braking, or traveling at the time.

Federal cargo rules address movement that adversely affects vehicle stability or maneuverability. See 49 CFR 393.100. Evidence must distinguish a load shift that contributed to a crash from movement caused by the impact itself.

Falling cargo: escape from the vehicle

Loose freight, building materials, equipment, or debris may create a hazard for people behind or beside the truck. Video, witness observations, and the location of items may help establish where the material came from and when it entered the roadway.

California Vehicle Code section 23114 generally requires vehicles to be constructed, covered, or loaded to prevent contents from escaping, subject to its exceptions and specific provisions. Read section 23114.

What do cargo-securement rules require?

For covered operations, federal standards address cargo containment and securement, including the systems and devices used to prevent dangerous movement. The requirements depend on the load; some commodities have specific rules. A generic strap count is not a reliable way to judge every shipment.

The FMCSA cargo-securement guide explains the general framework and commodity-specific standards. 49 CFR 393.106 addresses how articles must be immobilized or secured and includes requirements for items that can roll and for securement-system strength.

An investigator may examine restraints, attachment points, blocking or bracing, packaging, and the condition of the equipment. The right analysis depends on the actual cargo and applicable rules—not simply whether straps were visible in a photograph.

Federal and California requirements need to be evaluated for the particular vehicle and operation. A regulatory violation may be relevant evidence, but the connection to the collision and injuries still matters.

Must drivers check the load during a trip?

For drivers covered by the cargo-check requirements, federal rules call for an inspection within the first 50 miles and reexamination when duty status changes, after three hours of driving, or after 150 miles, whichever occurs first. Necessary adjustments are part of those duties.

There are important exceptions. These driver-check provisions do not apply to certain sealed vehicles that drivers have been ordered not to open, or loads arranged so inspection is impracticable. The exception does not answer every question about who loaded or secured the cargo. 49 CFR 392.9 contains the requirements and exceptions.

Trip records, stop information, inspection records, seal information, and loading instructions may help determine which requirements applied and what occurred.

Who may be responsible for improper loading?

The driver, motor carrier, shipper, warehouse, and loading contractor can have different roles. A familiar brand on a trailer does not identify every business involved.

  • Driver or motor carrier: loading knowledge, securement duties, applicable checks, and decisions to operate may matter.
  • Shipper, warehouse, or loading contractor: who actually placed, packaged, or secured the load, and whether a loading defect was apparent or concealed, may require review.
  • Equipment owner or maintenance provider: a relevant failure involving a trailer, restraint, or attachment point may call for investigation of control and maintenance.
  • Manufacturer or supplier: a suspected product defect requires its own evidence and legal analysis.

Responsibility is fact-specific. A company is not automatically liable because it owned the goods, and contracting out a task does not resolve every legal duty. Agreements, actual conduct, applicable law, and causation must be considered together. Read Trucking Company Liability.

Evidence that may explain the load

Useful evidence connects the shipment to the crash:

  • Bills of lading and manifests: identify the shipment, described contents, and businesses involved; stated weights may need independent confirmation.
  • Scale and weight records: help evaluate actual weight and axle distribution, including whether the record concerns the same load and stage of the trip.
  • Loading photographs and dock video: may show placement, restraints, and who performed the work.
  • Securement equipment and cargo: may help experts assess condition and failure, if safely preserved through appropriate arrangements.
  • Driver and dispatch communications: may reveal loading instructions, concerns, stops, or changes during the trip.
  • Scene video and witnesses: may establish whether cargo moved or fell before impact and how other vehicles reacted.
  • Medical and work records: help document injuries, treatment, and financial losses.

Records can be spread across multiple businesses. Timely preservation requests may need to reach the carrier, loading facility, equipment owner, and other relevant custodians. A request does not itself authorize access to private systems or compel production. See Truck Accident Evidence Preservation.

What to do after a cargo-related crash

Prioritize safety and medical care. Report an immediate roadway hazard or emergency to emergency services. Do not enter traffic, climb onto the truck, move unstable freight, or handle unknown substances to collect evidence.

From a safe location, preserve any photographs or video you already have, the truck's identifying information, witness details, and the crash report number. Write down what you observed: whether an item fell, where it came from, and what happened next. Separate your observations from assumptions.

Keep original files and insurer communications. If cargo has already been removed, tell the attorney what you know about the cleanup, storage, or disposal. Other evidence may remain. For broader practical guidance, see What to Do After a California Accident.

A brake failure claim starts with evidence

When a truck does not stop in time, a mechanical problem may be part of the explanation. But the collision alone does not establish brake failure, poor maintenance, or responsibility. The investigation needs to determine what happened, whether a defect existed before impact, and whether it contributed to the injuries.

The truck’s condition and its maintenance history should be examined together. Physical components may reveal a problem; inspection reports, repair records, and driver communications may show when it developed and who knew about it.

What may explain a truck braking problem?

An investigation may examine worn or damaged components, air-system problems, brake adjustment, overheating, or earlier repair work. The relevant components and tests depend on the truck and trailer’s actual brake systems.

Brake fade is a reduction in braking effectiveness associated with heat. California DMV explains that excessive brake use can cause overheating and fading or failure. That makes vehicle operation, road grade, and maintenance potentially relevant together. Read California DMV’s truck-driver guidance.

Investigators should also consider other explanations, such as speed, following distance, driver attention, road conditions, and the load. These factors can overlap. A defect found after a collision may have existed beforehand—or may have resulted from impact.

Federal rules generally require brakes with which a covered vehicle is equipped to remain operative, subject to specified exceptions. 49 CFR 393.48 explains the operative-brake requirement. Applying that rule to a particular truck requires review of the equipment and operation involved.

Three layers of inspection and maintenance

Routine maintenance: what was scheduled and completed?

For covered vehicles, federal rules require carriers to systematically inspect, repair, and maintain vehicles under their control. Relevant records can identify the vehicle, scheduled maintenance, and the dates and nature of inspections and repairs. 49 CFR 396.3 sets out these duties and record requirements.

A service invoice should be compared with the actual work, reported concerns, and later vehicle use. A document marked completed does not, by itself, answer whether a repair was adequate or whether a new defect arose afterward.

Driver checks and defect reports: what was noticed?

Before driving a covered vehicle, the driver must be satisfied that it is in safe operating condition and review the applicable previous inspection report as required. See 49 CFR 396.13.

Driver vehicle inspection reports can identify safety defects and document corrective action. Where the rule applies, a carrier must address listed defects likely to affect safe operation before permitting further operation and provide the required repair certification. Do not assume a written no-defect report must exist for every day: the federal rule does not require a report when no defect or deficiency is discovered or reported, and it includes additional exceptions. Read 49 CFR 396.11.

Periodic inspections: what was examined at that time?

Covered vehicles generally require a qualifying periodic inspection at least once within the preceding 12 months. 49 CFR 396.17 describes the periodic inspection requirement.

A passing inspection is relevant evidence of the inspection at that time. It does not establish that the truck remained safe indefinitely or eliminate the need for routine maintenance and attention to later defects.

Federal rules do not apply identically to every vehicle or operation. California requirements and applicable exceptions also need review.

Who may be responsible for poor maintenance?

The driver, carrier, vehicle owner, and repair provider may be different people or businesses. The investigation should identify each party’s role instead of assuming the name on the truck answers every question.

  • Motor carrier: its maintenance practices, response to defect reports, and decisions to keep a vehicle operating may matter.
  • Driver: required checks, reported symptoms, and the response to a known problem may be relevant.
  • Owner or lessor: agreements, control, and applicable duties should be examined; ownership alone does not settle the claim.
  • Maintenance or inspection provider: the scope and quality of work, findings, and qualifications may require review.
  • Manufacturer or supplier: a suspected product defect may call for a separate technical and legal investigation.

Federal regulations also address qualifications for personnel responsible for specified brake inspection, maintenance, service, or repair tasks. 49 CFR 396.25 explains the qualification requirements.

Outsourcing repairs does not end the inquiry into the carrier’s own duties. Conversely, hiring an outside shop does not automatically make that shop responsible for every later accident. A claim must connect a supported legal duty and relevant conduct or defect to the harm. See Trucking Company Liability.

Records that can connect a defect to the crash

A useful investigation asks specific questions rather than collecting paperwork without a purpose:

  • What condition existed? Vehicle examination, photographs, measurements, and preserved components may identify damage or wear.
  • When did the concern appear? Driver messages, defect reports, complaints, and service history may establish a timeline.
  • What work was performed? Repair orders, invoices, parts records, and technician notes may show what was addressed.
  • Who approved further operation? Repair certifications and dispatch communications may help explain decisions.
  • How did the truck move? Available video, witness accounts, scene evidence, and vehicle data may help reconstruct the sequence.
  • What losses followed? Medical records and work-loss documentation help explain the injuries and their effects.

Electronic logs and vehicle data serve different purposes. Do not assume a driving-hours log contains braking measurements, or that every truck stores useful crash data. The investigator must identify the system and its limitations.

Preserve the vehicle before evidence changes

Repairs, salvage, disposal, and later use can change the evidence. Prompt legal review can help identify the tractor, trailer, components, records, and data that should be preserved, and the parties who may control them.

A qualified inspection should be coordinated through appropriate arrangements. Photographs, identification of components, and documentation of how evidence is handled can help preserve its usefulness. Testing that changes or destroys a component requires careful planning and appropriate notice or agreement.

Do not enter a storage yard, crawl beneath a damaged truck, remove parts, or arrange unauthorized testing yourself. A preservation request is not permission to take possession or access a company’s systems. Read Truck Accident Evidence Preservation for more about preserving and obtaining records.

Record-retention periods are not waiting periods

Different federal records have different minimum retention rules:

  • Maintenance records: records covered by section 396.3 have a one-year retention requirement and must also be retained for six months after the vehicle leaves the carrier’s control. The recordkeeping provisions include conditions and exceptions. Source: 49 CFR 396.3.
  • Driver defect reports and certifications: covered records under section 396.11(a) must be retained for three months from report preparation. Source: 49 CFR 396.11.
  • Periodic inspection reports: section 396.21 requires retention for 14 months from the report date. Source: 49 CFR 396.21.

These rules do not guarantee that every useful record exists or remains available. Litigation-preservation obligations are a separate issue. Neither a retention period nor an insurer’s ongoing investigation extends your filing deadline. See California Accident Claim Deadlines.

What you can do now

Get appropriate medical care and keep your treatment records. Save original photographs, video, witness information, the report number, and insurer correspondence. If someone said the brakes failed, write down who said it, when, and the words you remember—separating that statement from your own observations.

Bring photographs of the truck, trailer, license plates, or identifying numbers if you already have them. You can seek a case evaluation even if the truck’s location or repair history is unknown.

A delivery crash can involve more than one business

After a collision with a delivery truck or commercial van, you may have the driver’s information but still not know which company operated the vehicle or which insurer should handle your claim. A familiar logo does not always identify the driver’s employer, the vehicle owner, or the business responsible for the trip.

The investigation should answer three questions: What caused the crash? Who may be legally responsible? What coverage may apply? Delivery records, employment relationships, and the driver’s activity at the time can help answer them.

What makes a delivery accident different?

Delivery operations can involve repeated stops, unfamiliar addresses, reversing into loading areas, turning across traffic, and pulling away from the curb. An investigation may examine visibility, parking position, speed, attention, vehicle condition, and instructions given to the driver.

A route schedule or delivery scanner may provide useful context, but a demanding route does not automatically prove negligence. The evidence must connect a particular action or failure to the collision and resulting harm.

These issues can arise with parcel vans, step vans, box trucks, grocery delivery vehicles, and vehicles used by local businesses. People injured may include other drivers, passengers, pedestrians, bicyclists, or workers near a delivery area.

Who may be responsible for the crash?

The driver and the driver’s employer

A driver may be responsible for negligent driving that causes injury. An employer may also be responsible when an employee causes harm while acting within the scope of employment. The assigned route, delivery timing, dispatch communications, and actual activity at the time can help establish that relationship. California civil jury instruction 3701 explains employer and principal responsibility.

A business’s own unsafe conduct

An investigation may separately examine hiring, supervision, vehicle maintenance, or delivery instructions. For example, relevant records might show that a business knew of an unsafe vehicle condition but did not address it.

Negligent hiring or retention requires more than the fact that a driver had an accident. Knowledge of unfitness or incompetence, a resulting particular risk, and a causal connection to the harm are among the issues that must be established. California civil jury instruction 426 describes the requirements.

Other businesses involved in the operation

A vehicle owner, maintenance provider, loading business, or other entity may warrant review when its conduct and legal duties are relevant. The retailer receiving or selling the goods is not automatically responsible simply because its products were being delivered.

For more detail about responsibility beyond the driver, read Trucking Company Liability.

What if the driver works for a contractor or delivery app?

A delivery can involve a national brand, a local delivery contractor, and a driver working under a separate agreement. A driver may also use a personally owned vehicle for deliveries arranged through an app.

The investigation should identify the legal businesses involved, who assigned the work, and the actual relationship between the parties. Contracts, dispatch records, payment arrangements, and evidence of control may matter. A contractor label alone does not resolve every liability issue; neither does wearing a branded uniform.

For app-based deliveries, preserve information about the specific order and timing when available. Whether the driver had accepted a delivery, was traveling to collect it, or had completed it may matter under the applicable policy. Do not assume passenger rideshare insurance rules apply to package or food delivery. The service, policy language, and circumstances require separate review.

Commercial use does not answer every coverage question.

The specific policy and delivery activity matter.

CALIFORNIA TODAY.
STRONGER TOMORROW.

Which insurance may apply?

Liability and insurance coverage are related but separate questions. A business can dispute responsibility, an insurer can dispute coverage, or both can happen in the same claim.

Business-owned trucks and vans

A commercial auto policy may cover a business-owned vehicle, subject to the policy’s insured parties, covered vehicles, terms, exclusions, and limits. Additional policies may need review, but a commercial vehicle does not guarantee a particular recovery or insurance limit.

Rented vehicles and employee-owned vehicles

When a business rents a van or a worker uses a personal vehicle, the investigation may need to examine rental agreements, personal coverage, and any business coverage for hired or non-owned vehicles. Coverage protecting the business does not necessarily protect every driver in the same way.

Personal vehicles used for deliveries

Personal auto coverage may restrict or exclude some delivery or business uses. Delivery-specific coverage or a platform policy may also exist. Obtain the applicable policy information and any written coverage explanation rather than relying only on an insurance card or verbal assurance.

The California Department of Insurance commercial insurance guide explains why commercial auto exposures can require specialized coverage. Its auto insurance guide also explains basic coverage types and policy limits.

If available coverage is insufficient, your own insurance may need review. See Uninsured and Underinsured Motorist Claims. Eligibility depends on the applicable policy and law.

Does every delivery van follow federal trucking rules?

No. Business use alone does not establish that every federal motor-carrier rule applies. Vehicle weight, the type of transportation, cargo, and applicable exceptions can affect the analysis. California requirements may apply separately.

The federal commercial motor vehicle definition illustrates why a vehicle’s classification requires more than looking at its logo or shape. Likewise, federal financial-responsibility requirements distinguish among covered operations and cargo. Those requirements should not be presented as a universal insurance amount for every delivery van.

Do not assume a smaller van has an electronic driving log or that every vehicle records usable crash data. Investigators should identify the equipment and systems actually used.

Evidence that may help explain the delivery

Different records answer different questions:

  • Vehicle and operator identity: photographs of plates, company names, identifying numbers, and the truck or van help identify the operation.
  • Work assignment: route sheets, dispatch messages, delivery timestamps, and relevant order records may show the purpose of the trip.
  • Crash sequence: dash-camera footage, nearby business video, witness accounts, and scene photographs may help establish what happened.
  • Vehicle condition: inspection and repair records may matter if a mechanical problem contributed.
  • Relationships and coverage: driver agreements, rental documents, policies, and insurer correspondence may help identify responsible parties and coverage.
  • Injuries and losses: medical records, missed-work information, and documentation of daily limitations help explain the crash’s effects.

Save originals of files you already have. Video and operational data can be overwritten, so timely preservation matters. A preservation request does not itself grant access to a company’s systems or compel production of documents.

See Truck Accident Evidence Preservation for the distinction between saving records and obtaining them through appropriate legal procedures.

What should I do after a delivery vehicle accident?

  • Move to safety when possible and call emergency services if needed. Seek appropriate medical attention.
  • Exchange driver, vehicle, and insurance information when it is safe to do so.
  • Photograph the vehicle, company markings, damage, and surrounding area without entering traffic or private property.
  • Save witness details, the crash report number, and relevant messages or order information.
  • Notify your own insurer as required by your policy and keep copies of claim communications.
  • Get advice before signing a release, particularly if the full extent of your injuries is not yet understood.

California DMV requires an SR-1 report within 10 days when a crash causes injury, death, or more than $1,000 in property damage. This is a separate requirement from a police or insurance report. Use the DMV’s accident-reporting guidance.

Do not wait for a company to finish its internal investigation before checking your legal deadlines. Different rules may apply to government vehicles or public entities. Read California Accident Claim Deadlines and obtain advice about your specific circumstances.

Trucking Company Liability in California

Look beyond the driver. Follow the evidence.

Who assigned the trip, maintained the truck, and made the safety decisions?

01Identify the relationships
02Examine company decisions
03Connect evidence to the crash

IN THIS GUIDE

Two paths to company responsibility

Company involvement alone does not establish liability.

Maintenance and inspection

Dispatch and trip records

Responsibility may extend beyond the driver

After a serious truck crash, the driver’s actions are only part of the picture. Who assigned the trip? Who maintained the truck? Was the driver qualified for the work? Those questions may reveal responsibility beyond the person behind the wheel.

A trucking company may be responsible for a driver’s negligence within the scope of employment, or for its own negligent decisions that helped cause the collision. Other businesses may also need to be investigated. Company involvement alone does not establish liability: the legal relationship, applicable duties, and connection to your injuries matter.

USEFUL SOURCES

Cornell Law: carrier dutiesCalifornia Courts: evidence

Two ways a trucking company may be responsible

Responsibility for a driver’s work-related negligence

An employer can be legally responsible for harm caused by an employee’s negligence while acting within the scope of employment. This is often called vicarious liability. A separate company safety violation is not necessarily required for this route to liability.

The investigation may examine who employed or controlled the driver, the assigned work, and what the driver was doing when the crash occurred. A delivery assignment, dispatch messages, and trip records may help establish that relationship. Whether a particular detour or activity was within the scope of employment depends on the facts. California civil jury instruction 3701 explains the employer or principal liability framework.

Responsibility for the company’s own negligence

A separate question is whether the company’s own conduct contributed to the harm. For example, did it retain a driver despite known safety problems, ignore a repair issue, or impose an unsafe schedule?

Negligent hiring, supervision, or retention requires more than showing that an employee caused a crash. Relevant issues include whether the employer knew or should have known of unfitness or incompetence that created a particular risk, and whether its negligence was a substantial factor in causing harm. California civil jury instruction 426 describes these elements.

These are distinct legal theories. Which claims should be pursued depends on the evidence and the company’s position in the case.

Company decisions that may deserve investigation

Driver qualifications and safety concerns

Applications, driving-history reviews, qualification records, training materials, and earlier safety complaints may help show what the company knew and when. A prior incident is not automatically proof of negligence in your crash; its relevance and admissibility require review.

For covered operations, federal rules prohibit a carrier from requiring or permitting an unqualified person to drive a commercial motor vehicle. Qualifications address matters including licensing, experience or training, and physical qualification, subject to applicable exceptions. Read 49 CFR 391.11 through Cornell Law School.

Dispatch instructions and delivery schedules

Dispatch messages, appointment times, route assignments, and duty records can help test whether the schedule and instructions supported safe operation. A demanding deadline does not, by itself, prove that it caused a crash.

Federal rules prohibit carriers from scheduling or requiring a run in a time that would necessitate unlawful speeds. 49 CFR 392.6 addresses delivery schedules and speed limits. Another rule places responsibility on carriers to require observance of covered driver duties and prohibitions. See 49 CFR 390.11.

Inspection, maintenance, and repairs

Brake, tire, steering, or other equipment issues may require inspection of the vehicle and review of maintenance records. Useful questions include whether a defect existed before the crash, who knew about it, who was responsible for repairs, and whether it contributed to the collision.

Federal regulations require covered carriers to systematically inspect, repair, and maintain vehicles subject to their control. 49 CFR 396.3 explains the maintenance duty and associated records. Outsourcing a repair does not eliminate the need to examine the carrier’s own duties as well as the repair provider’s conduct.

Federal requirements vary by operation and exemptions. California requirements may also apply. A violation is an issue to analyze—not an automatic finding that the company caused your injuries.

What if the driver is an independent contractor?

An independent-contractor label does not end the investigation. The driver agreement, equipment lease, operating authority, actual working relationship, and circumstances of the trip may all matter. The tractor owner, trailer owner, and motor carrier can be different businesses.

For covered leases, federal regulations require provisions giving the authorized carrier possession, control, and responsibility for the equipment during the lease. The same regulation expressly says those provisions do not determine whether the lessor or driver is an employee or independent contractor. Read the distinction in 49 CFR 376.12(c).

Do not assume the company is protected because the driver received a particular tax form. Equally, do not assume a company name or USDOT number on the truck resolves every liability question.

Who else may share responsibility?

Owners, repair providers, and other businesses require a fact-specific review.

Which other businesses may need review?

  • Truck or trailer owner: ownership, leasing arrangements, maintenance responsibilities, and applicable legal duties may matter.
  • Repair or inspection provider: work orders and physical evidence may help determine whether negligent work contributed to a failure.
  • Shipper or loading company: loading records and cargo evidence may be relevant when the load’s placement or securement played a role.
  • Manufacturer or component supplier: a suspected product defect requires its own technical and legal analysis.
  • Broker or other transportation intermediary: contractual labels and actual conduct need review; federal law can limit some claims.

These are investigation possibilities, not a list of businesses automatically responsible for every crash. Each proposed claim needs a supported legal basis and a connection to the harm.

Evidence that connects the company to the crash

An effective investigation connects records to specific questions:

  • Who was operating the trip? Dispatch instructions, shipping documents, employment agreements, and equipment leases may identify roles.
  • Was the driver qualified and supervised? Qualification files, training records, and relevant safety communications may provide context.
  • Was the vehicle properly maintained? Inspection reports, defect notices, repair invoices, and an appropriate vehicle examination may help.
  • What happened before impact? Available video, witness accounts, trip records, and vehicle data may help establish the sequence.
  • How did the crash affect you? Medical records, work information, and documentation of daily limitations help connect injuries and losses to the event.

Different systems preserve different information. Electronic driving logs are not interchangeable with vehicle crash data, and no device should be assumed to contain every answer.

Preservation requests should identify relevant records and equipment promptly. A request to preserve evidence does not itself compel production or give access to a company’s systems. Lawyers may need appropriate discovery procedures to obtain records. California Courts explains requests for documents and other evidence.

For a practical guide to logs, video, inspection records, and preservation requests, see Truck Accident Evidence Preservation.

What you can do now

  • Get appropriate medical attention and keep your treatment records.
  • Save photographs already taken of company names, identifying numbers, license plates, and vehicle damage.
  • Keep the crash report number, witness details, insurer letters, and original video files.
  • Write down what you personally remember, separating observations from guesses.
  • Seek advice before signing a release or authorizing disposal of potentially relevant evidence.

Do not enter a truck yard, access another person’s account, or approach an unsafe vehicle to gather evidence. You do not need to investigate the company yourself before seeking help.

Multiple companies do not guarantee a larger recovery

Identifying a responsible business can affect available claims and insurance, but a company’s size does not establish the value of a case. Recovery depends on proven liability, injuries and losses, applicable coverage, available assets, and other case-specific issues. Overlapping policies do not necessarily provide separate recoveries for the same loss.

Medical expenses, lost earnings, future care, and the effects on everyday life may require careful documentation. Learn more in Compensation Available After an Accident and Partial Fault in a California Accident.

Protect the records that may explain the crash

After a truck collision, important evidence may be held by the carrier, a vehicle owner, a repair facility, or a technology provider. Video may be overwritten, a truck may return to service, and damaged parts may be replaced. A prompt review can identify what may exist and who should be asked to preserve it.

MMG Law Firm can discuss the crash, potential evidence sources, and appropriate next steps. You do not need to know the trucking company’s data systems before calling.

Start with the truck, the time, and the location

Safety and medical care come first. When you can safely gather information, keep the crash date, approximate time, location, police agency, and report number. Photographs of the carrier name, USDOT number, license plates, and tractor and trailer numbers can help identify the right vehicle and record holders. Do not approach a truck in active traffic to obtain them.

Save your own original photos, recordings, witness details, and insurer correspondence. Tell the reviewing attorney if a vehicle is scheduled for repair, sale, salvage, or disposal. An inspection may need coordination; do not attempt to remove equipment or download another person’s vehicle yourself. See what to do after a California accident.

Key records may be subject to specific time limits.

6 months

Other evidence

Video and vehicle data may follow different rules.

Selected federal rules. Coverage and exceptions apply. Preservation duties may require longer retention.

Different records answer different questions

Electronic logs: duty status and driving time

Electronic logging devices, or ELDs, support hours-of-service records. They may help show when a driver recorded driving, on-duty, off-duty, or sleeper-berth time. Relevant supporting records can help test the timeline and identify inconsistencies.

An ELD is not automatically a detailed crash recorder. FMCSA explains that ELDs are not required to collect speed, braking, steering, or other vehicle-performance parameters. Some fleet systems collect additional information, but that must be investigated separately. Read FMCSA’s ELD questions and answers.

Log compliance alone does not prove a driver was alert, and a log violation alone does not establish that it caused the crash. Logs must be compared with the other evidence.

Vehicle data: what the truck’s systems may retain

Engine-control modules, event recorders, braking systems, or telematics platforms may hold useful information, depending on the equipment. Available data may relate to speed, braking, engine activity, fault codes, or location. There is no universal truck “black box” that records every detail of every crash.

An appropriate specialist may need to identify the system, preserve available data, and document the collection method. Movement, repairs, module replacement, or later events may affect some records. The exact risks depend on the system; do not assume all data disappear in the same way or after the same interval.

Video: the truck, nearby vehicles, and surrounding properties

Dash cameras, inward-facing cameras, nearby businesses, and other vehicles may provide different views. Not every camera records continuously, and some systems store only selected events. Identify possible sources quickly, including the relevant time window before and after the collision.

A clip can omit what happened just outside its frame. Preserve the original file, available timing information, and surrounding footage where relevant. Camera clocks may need comparison with other records.

Inspection and maintenance records: reported problems and repairs

Driver vehicle inspection reports, periodic inspection reports, work orders, and repair histories may help identify reported brake, tire, lighting, or other equipment concerns. A recorded defect is not automatic proof of causation, and a clean inspection report does not establish the vehicle’s condition at the moment of impact.

Federal rules require covered carriers to systematically inspect, repair, and maintain equipment. 49 CFR 396.3 describes the maintenance and recordkeeping requirements.

Dispatch, cargo, and trip records

Relevant dispatch messages, delivery instructions, bills of lading, weight records, and loading or securement information may help explain the trip. Their importance depends on the issues: timing, route, cargo movement, or the roles of different businesses. A preservation request should identify relevant categories rather than assume every company holds every record.

How long must trucking records be kept?

There is no single retention period for all truck evidence. The following are selected federal requirements for records and operations covered by the cited rules, not a complete list:

  • Duty-status records and supporting documents: Generally six months from receipt under 49 CFR 395.8(k). FMCSA also requires a separate-device backup of ELD records for six months; see its ELD retention guidance.
  • Covered maintenance records: One year, and six months after the vehicle leaves the carrier’s control, under 49 CFR 396.3(c). The recordkeeping provision generally concerns vehicles controlled for 30 consecutive days, with stated exceptions.
  • Required driver vehicle inspection reports and related certifications: Three months from preparation under 49 CFR 396.11(a)(4). Exceptions and report requirements matter; the rule does not require a report when no defect or deficiency is discovered or reported in the circumstances it describes.
  • Periodic inspection reports: Fourteen months from the report date under 49 CFR 396.21.

These periods do not mean you should wait. They do not guarantee that a particular video, electronic event, or physical component will remain available. Separate litigation-preservation obligations may require relevant material to be kept longer than routine recordkeeping periods.

Federal and California requirements depend on the operation and applicable exceptions. CHP explains California’s requirements for intrastate electronic logging devices. A truck operating within California is not automatically exempt from electronic logging requirements.

What does a preservation request do?

A preservation request identifies a collision and asks a person or business to retain potentially relevant evidence. It can put the recipient on notice of a claim and identify records at risk of deletion, alteration, repair, or disposal.

Preservation is different from access. A letter is not a subpoena or court order. It does not automatically permit an inspection, require immediate production, or give you access to private accounts. Obtaining records may require agreement, formal discovery, a subpoena, or court action. California Courts explains discovery requests and third-party subpoenas.

A preservation duty can arise before a letter is sent, depending on the circumstances and applicable law. Conversely, sending a letter does not guarantee that material exists, will be preserved, or can be recovered if already lost.

What a focused request may address

  • The crash date, location, involved driver, and identifying vehicle information.
  • Relevant record categories and a justified time range.
  • The tractor, trailer, involved components, and known electronic systems.
  • Original files, available metadata, relevant edits, and audit history.
  • Relevant copies held by employees, vendors, or service providers.
  • Suspension of routine deletion for identified relevant material and coordination before changes that may affect an inspection.

The right recipients and scope depend on the facts. They may include the carrier, vehicle owner, repair or storage facility, and relevant technology or video providers. A request should not unnecessarily seek unrelated personal information or interfere with emergency safety measures.

Why original files and collection records matter

A screenshot or short exported clip may leave out information needed to understand the record. Where appropriate, preserve native files and keep track of when, how, and by whom copies were collected. Preserve originals without annotation and use separate working copies for notes.

Differences in time zones, clock settings, vehicle identifiers, or file versions can affect interpretation. A reliable timeline may require comparison among logs, video, vehicle data, dispatch records, and witness accounts. No single record necessarily resolves fault or injury causation.

What if evidence has already been deleted or changed?

Missing evidence does not automatically end a claim or prove misconduct. Copies may exist with another custodian, and other evidence may answer the same question. It can be important to establish what existed, when it changed, who controlled it, and whether a preservation duty applied.

Legal consequences for loss or destruction of evidence depend on the facts and governing rules; sanctions are not automatic. Tell counsel about known repairs, deletion notices, or disposal dates, and preserve those communications. Do not alter your own relevant records, including material that appears unfavorable.

A chain-reaction collision can leave you dealing with injuries, a damaged vehicle, and several insurers pointing toward someone else. You may remember being hit more than once without knowing which driver started the sequence.

MMG Law Firm can review the available evidence, help identify potentially responsible parties, and explain the insurance questions affecting your claim. You do not need to resolve the disagreement between drivers before contacting the firm.

Who is responsible in a chain-reaction crash?

Responsibility depends on how the collision unfolded and whose conduct contributed to the injuries. The last driver in line is not automatically responsible for every impact. A vehicle’s final position does not, by itself, establish the order of collisions.

An investigation may examine following distance, speed, braking, lane changes, distraction, visibility, roadway conditions, and whether one vehicle was pushed into another. More than one person’s negligence may contribute to the same harm. California’s multiple-cause jury instruction, CACI 431, explains that another contributing cause does not necessarily relieve a negligent defendant of responsibility.

Why the order of impacts matters

Illustrative example, not an MMG case: Three vehicles are stopped or slowing in a line. If the rear vehicle pushes the middle vehicle into the front vehicle, the investigation differs from a situation in which the middle vehicle strikes first and is then hit from behind. The damage may look similar afterward, but the sequence can affect responsibility and the connection between each impact and the claimed injuries.

That distinction must be supported by evidence. An insurer’s initial diagram or a driver’s confident account is not a substitute for examining the full record.
