Reconstructing the sequence when accounts conflict

Compare what each person could actually observe

A driver may feel two impacts without seeing what happened behind them. A witness may observe only the final collision. Record what you saw, heard, and felt, and distinguish those observations from what you learned later. Do not guess the number of seconds between impacts if you do not know.

Preserve video and photographs

Original dashcam files and nearby camera footage may help show braking, vehicle movement, and the sequence. Photographs can document damage on every side, debris, road markings, and final positions. Footage may be overwritten, and not every traffic camera records. Identify possible sources promptly without entering traffic or private property to collect evidence.

Review vehicle information in context

Available event data may help specialists examine speed changes or braking around a collision. Vehicle capabilities, recording limits, and the particular event affect what is available. No single download necessarily captures the entire chain reaction. NHTSA explains event data recorders and their short recording windows.

Connect the collision evidence to the injury evidence

Medical records, symptoms reported after the crash, prior health history, and appropriate expert analysis may help evaluate injury causation. A patient should describe their experience accurately rather than assign a diagnosis or a particular injury to one impact without medical support.

Police reports, witness accounts, video, vehicle damage, and medical information can complement or contradict one another. The goal is a supported explanation, not simply a larger stack of records.

What to do while the insurers investigate

  • Prioritize safety and treatment. Call 911 for an emergency. Avoid standing between vehicles or entering active traffic to take photographs.
  • Identify each vehicle and insurer. Keep driver names, vehicle descriptions, insurance information, and the police report number when available.
  • Write down your own recollection. Note whether your vehicle was moving, stopped, or pushed, and what you remember about separate impacts.
  • Preserve original files. Save recordings and photos without editing or deleting the originals. Tell counsel if a vehicle may be repaired, sold, or disposed of before an inspection.
  • Maintain one claim log. List each insurer, claim number, adjuster, contact date, and requested document. Save letters and messages.
  • Report to your insurer promptly. Policy notice and cooperation requirements can apply. Keep your statements factual and say when you do not know an answer.

California DMV requires an SR-1 report within 10 days when a collision causes injury, death, or more than $1,000 in property damage. This is separate from a police report or insurance claim. Check DMV’s SR-1 reporting requirements. See also what to do after a California accident.

How do claims involving several insurers work?

Different policies may address different losses. Each insurer may investigate its insured’s role, coverage, and the extent of your damages. One company accepting a vehicle-repair claim does not necessarily resolve every injury claim.

Liability claims against other drivers

Potential claims depend on responsibility and applicable coverage. With several injured people, an available per-accident limit may have to address competing claims. Multiple vehicles do not guarantee multiple full policy-limit payments.

Coverage under your own policy

Depending on the policy, collision coverage may help with vehicle repairs, medical payments coverage may address qualifying medical expenses, and uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage may be relevant. Deductibles, exclusions, limits, offsets, and settlement conditions can matter. Read MMG’s uninsured and underinsured motorist guide.

Coordination before settlement

Keep track of who paid what. Insurers or health plans may assert reimbursement rights, and payments can affect the remaining claim. Do not assume you can collect twice for the same loss or simply add every policy limit together. The California Department of Insurance coverage guide explains the main coverage types and limits.

If one insurer asks for a statement, clarify whom it represents and why it needs the information. Your obligations to your own insurer can differ from requests by another driver’s insurer. For an overview of claim handling, read the Department of Insurance accident guide.

What if more than one person shares fault?

California allows responsibility to be allocated among people whose negligence contributed to the harm. If your own negligence contributed, it may reduce your recovery rather than necessarily bar it. CACI 406 addresses apportionment of responsibility.

The rules governing how damages are collected from different defendants are more involved than dividing every bill by a single fault percentage. They can depend on the type of damages, the injuries each defendant caused, settlements, and applicable law. Read partial fault in a California accident.

If you were a passenger, potential claims may involve more than one driver, including the driver of the vehicle you occupied. Passengers and drivers do not always have identical legal interests; representation should account for possible conflicts.

What injury-severity research can contribute

The methods excerpt supplied for the linked review of two-vehicle and multi-vehicle crash injury severity describes a structured literature search across transportation and health databases. It groups relevant research around driver characteristics, vehicle attributes, roadway infrastructure, environmental conditions, and crash-related factors.

For someone documenting a collision, those categories offer a useful way to organize questions: What were the vehicles doing? What vehicles were involved? What were the road, lighting, and weather conditions? What happened during each impact? This is a practical application of the categories, not a finding that any one factor caused your injuries.

Research limits: The supplied passage describes search and selection methods, not the review’s results. It does not establish fault, diagnose an injury, rank the causes of your crash, or predict compensation. Injury-severity models describe patterns in study data; individual claims still require case-specific evidence. The full article’s findings have not been independently verified for this draft.

Review every release before resolving part of the case

An offer from one insurer may involve terms affecting claims against other people or available coverage. Review which parties are released, which claims are resolved, whether any rights are reserved, and how liens or reimbursement claims affect the amount you receive.

A property-damage payment and an injury settlement are not automatically the same thing, but the wording of the agreement matters. See insurance settlement offers and releases and medical bills, liens, and treatment costs.

Deadlines continue while fault is disputed

California personal-injury lawsuits generally must be filed within two years, subject to exceptions. Claims involving a government entity commonly require a claim within six months for personal injury, followed by separate lawsuit requirements. Coverage-related deadlines may also apply.

Do not assume that an insurer’s investigation or negotiations extend the time to act. California Courts explains personal-injury filing deadlines. Read California accident claim deadlines and seek advice promptly when a public vehicle or roadway condition may be involved.

IN THIS GUIDE

What was happening before the crash?

Multiple types of evidence can help show what a driver was doing and when.

Video and witnesses

Traffic cameras, dash cams, and witness statements can show driver behavior before the crash.

Phone and device records

Call logs, text messages, and app activity can help establish timing and phone use.

Vehicle and work records

Vehicle data, fleet records, and employment records may show distraction and work-related activity.

A moment of distraction can leave lasting consequences

You may have seen the other driver looking down. A witness may have noticed a phone. Or the crash may have happened without any obvious explanation. You do not need to prove distraction before asking for help.

MMG Law Firm can review what happened, identify evidence worth preserving, and explain your options after a California car, truck, or motorcycle collision. The important question is whether a driver’s failure to pay attention contributed to the crash and your injuries.

Request a free case evaluation or call (818) 539-7969. No recovery, no attorney fees or case expenses owed to MMG. Medical bills and other third-party obligations are separate.

What counts as distracted driving?

Distraction can take a driver’s eyes off the road, hands away from driving, or attention away from traffic. Examples include reading messages, handling a phone, adjusting navigation, reaching for an object, eating, or focusing on passengers. Texting can combine all three kinds of distraction. NHTSA explains these different forms of distraction.

A phone is not required for a distracted-driving claim. Equally, a phone in the vehicle does not establish that its driver was distracted. The investigation must connect the driver’s conduct to the collision.

Why distraction can be missed

Cornell discusses the challenge of identifying distraction after a crash.

Historical data and survey findings do not establish fault in an individual case.

What California data and research tell us

The California Office of Traffic Safety reports that 148 people died in California crashes involving a distracted driver in 2022, down 5.1% from 2021. Separately, its 2025 public-opinion survey found that 71.4% of Californians identified texting-related distraction as one of their top traffic-safety concerns. The first figure is a historical fatality count; the second measures public concern, not the percentage of crashes caused by texting. Read the OTS distracted-driving overview.

Cornell University’s Evidence Based Living article discusses research on distraction and explains why it can be difficult to identify during crash investigations. Its discussion of national fatalities refers to 2021 data, not a current-year total. It also describes how distraction can affect a driver’s eyes, hands, or attention.

These sources provide safety context. They do not establish that a particular driver was distracted, determine legal responsibility, or predict a settlement. Your claim depends on evidence about your collision and injuries.

How can distraction be investigated and proven?

Different records answer different questions. A useful investigation compares independent sources and checks whether their timing, viewpoint, and meaning support the same account.

Witnesses and statements

A passenger, nearby driver, or pedestrian may have seen someone looking down, holding a device, or failing to react. The witness’s location, lighting, viewing time, and exact observations matter. Seeing a lowered head does not necessarily establish texting. Preserve contact details and the words you remember without asking anyone to guess.

Dash cameras and nearby video

Footage may show lane movement, traffic signals, braking, or visible driver behavior. It may also contradict an initial impression. Identify nearby businesses, residences, buses, and vehicles that could have recorded the scene. Availability and retention vary; do not assume every traffic camera records or stores footage.

Phone and device records

Relevant call or message records may help establish a timeline. They may not show message content, every app interaction, who was using the device, or whether the driver was looking at the screen. Background activity and differences between device clocks require careful interpretation.

NHTSA’s investigation guide explains that some app messages do not appear in carrier text records and that precise timing matters. It is a guide for criminal investigators and prosecutors; it does not give a civil attorney the same investigative powers. Read the NHTSA investigation guide.

Vehicle data and crash reconstruction

An event data recorder may provide a short record of speed, braking, or other vehicle information, depending on the vehicle and event. It generally does not establish what a driver was reading or thinking. A qualified specialist may compare available data with photographs, damage, roadway conditions, and video. NHTSA explains event data recorders.

Work-related records

For a driver working at the time, relevant dispatch messages, delivery activity, fleet video, or employer records may deserve review. Their availability depends on the facts and lawful access. A work-related trip can raise additional responsibility questions; it does not automatically make every employer or platform liable.

Can a lawyer obtain the other driver’s phone records?

Sometimes relevant records can be obtained, but access is not automatic. In a lawsuit, an attorney may use document requests, subpoenas, or other appropriate procedures. The source of the records, privacy rights, legal restrictions, objections, and court orders can limit disclosure. A subpoena does not guarantee access to message contents or an entire phone.

The California Courts discovery guide distinguishes requests to parties from subpoenas to third parties. A focused request should seek evidence relevant to the crash, rather than unrelated personal information.

Preserving evidence and obtaining it are separate steps. A preservation request may help protect available material while access is addressed, but cannot restore data that no longer exists. Do not access another person’s accounts or devices yourself.

What should I preserve now?

  • Care and safety first: Get appropriate medical care. Call 911 for an emergency or immediate danger.
  • Original recordings: Save original dashcam files and photographs, including surrounding footage where available. Keep an unedited copy.
  • Witness information: Record names, contact details, locations, and what each person actually observed.
  • Crash details: Note the date, approximate time, location, vehicles, police agency, and report number.
  • Potential video sources: Write down nearby camera locations so preservation can be considered promptly.
  • Your own records: Keep relevant messages, receipts, medical paperwork, and work-loss records. Do not delete potentially relevant material because it seems unfavorable.

Tell the reviewing attorney if a vehicle is about to be repaired or disposed of, or if a device or recording may be lost. Avoid delaying necessary treatment or safety measures to collect evidence. See what to do after a California accident.

California phone rules and civil responsibility

California generally restricts holding and operating a phone while driving. Hands-free operation and limited interaction with a properly mounted device are subject to specific requirements. Drivers under 18 face stricter restrictions. Emergency exceptions and the circumstances of use may matter. The California Highway Patrol explains hands-free driving rules.

Complying with a phone rule does not excuse otherwise careless driving. A hands-free conversation or an unrelated distraction can still be relevant if it interfered with safe driving. The CHP distracted-driving program discusses both phone and non-phone distractions.

In a typical negligence claim, the evidence must establish negligent conduct, harm, and the required causal connection. California’s civil jury instructions address driver care, causation, and comparative fault in CACI 700, 430, and 405. Explore the Judicial Council’s civil jury instructions.

A traffic citation can be relevant, but does not automatically prove a civil claim. The absence of a citation does not automatically defeat one. Rear-end damage, lack of visible braking, or an unanswered message alone does not conclusively establish distraction.

What if the insurer disputes fault or my injuries?

The insurer may question who caused the crash, whether a record shows driver activity, or whether the collision caused the claimed injuries. A careful response connects the crash evidence with medical findings, treatment history, and the practical effects on your life.

If you were also negligent and that negligence contributed to your harm, California comparative-fault rules may reduce your recovery by your assigned share. Partial responsibility does not necessarily prevent recovery. Read partial fault in a California accident.

Depending on the evidence, damages may include medical expenses, future care, lost income, reduced earning capacity, and pain and suffering. A distraction allegation does not produce an automatic settlement amount or automatic punitive damages. See compensation available after an accident and medical bills, liens, and treatment costs.

How long do I have to take action?

California personal-injury lawsuits generally have a two-year filing deadline, but important exceptions apply. Claims involving a public entity commonly require an earlier government claim, generally within six months for personal injury. Separate lawsuit deadlines can follow. The correct deadline depends on the parties and facts.

The California Courts personal-injury guide explains the general time limit. Evidence may disappear much sooner than a filing deadline. Insurance discussions do not necessarily extend the time to sue. Review California accident claim deadlines promptly.

COMMON QUESTIONS

Your recovery deserves a clear next step

After a crash involving a suspected impaired driver, you may face medical bills, missed work, insurance calls, and questions about a criminal investigation. A civil injury claim can address losses caused by another person’s wrongful conduct. It follows its own process, even when police and prosecutors are also involved.

MMG Law Firm helps people evaluate California accident claims from its Glendale office. An evaluation can address the evidence, available insurance, deadlines, and the effect of a proposed settlement.

Call (818) 539-7969 or request a free case evaluation. No recovery, no attorney fees or case expenses owed to MMG. Medical bills and other third-party obligations are separate.

What to do after a suspected impaired-driving crash

Prioritize safety and medical care. Call 911 for an emergency or an immediate danger. Tell responding officers what you actually observed; do not confront, follow, or attempt to test a driver yourself.

  • Exchange driver, vehicle, and insurance information when safe.
  • Keep the police agency’s name, report number, and any available criminal case information.
  • Save original photographs and dashcam footage, including the period before and after impact.
  • Obtain witness contact details and preserve their independent observations.
  • Keep treatment records, work restrictions, receipts, and insurer correspondence.
  • Notify your insurer as your policy requires and retain copies of communications.

California DMV requires an SR-1 within 10 days for a crash involving injury, death, or property damage over $1,000. This is separate from a police report. Review DMV accident-reporting instructions and what to do after a California accident.

A DUI arrest does not guarantee a civil payout.

Evidence, coverage, and legal requirements still matter. Punitive damages require additional proof.

A civil claim and a DUI prosecution are different

The criminal case

Prosecutors decide whether to pursue charges. Criminal proceedings address alleged offenses and may result in penalties and victim restitution. Your injury lawyer does not control charging decisions or guarantee a conviction.

The civil injury claim

A civil claim seeks compensation from legally responsible parties or applicable insurance. It must address responsibility, causation, and legally recoverable losses. The ordinary civil negligence burden differs from the criminal standard, and specific issues can carry different proof requirements.

An arrest alone does not prove every part of a civil claim. Conversely, the absence of an arrest or conviction does not automatically defeat one. The effect of a plea, conviction, dismissal, or other criminal ruling requires individual legal analysis.

Do not wait for a criminal case to finish before checking civil deadlines. Learn about California victims’ rights and how an accident claim works.

What must the evidence show?

The evidence must connect wrongful conduct to the collision and the injuries claimed. Impairment may be important, but it does not eliminate the need to investigate how the crash happened or document the resulting harm.

California’s Judicial Council instruction explains impairment by asking whether alcohol, drugs, or their combined effects impaired safe driving ability to an appreciable degree. Read CACI 709 on driving under the influence.

Drug-related impairment can involve prescription or over-the-counter medication as well as illegal drugs. A lawful prescription does not establish that a person was safe to drive. Equally, the presence of a substance does not by itself answer every question about impairment, timing, or causation. See the California DMV alcohol and drugs guide.

Records that may matter

Collision and impairment evidence

Depending on availability and lawful access, relevant material may include officer observations, witness accounts, video, chemical-test records, dispatch records, photographs, and vehicle information. Testing time, procedures, and interpretation may require qualified expert review. Do not assume that all investigation records are immediately available to you.

Describe observations rather than conclusions: what the vehicle did, what you heard, and what you saw. Preserve original files and correspondence. Footage can be overwritten, and evidence may become harder to obtain as time passes.

Injury and loss evidence

Medical records, diagnosis, treatment recommendations, income records, and documented limitations help explain the consequences of the collision. Give providers an accurate history, including relevant prior conditions. Keep factual notes about missed work and assistance you need, without exaggerating symptoms or guessing at future costs.

Serious injuries may require analysis of future care and reduced earning capacity. See catastrophic injuries, traumatic brain injury, and medical bills and treatment costs.

What compensation may be available?

Depending on the facts and applicable law, compensatory damages may include medical expenses, reasonably supported future care, lost earnings, reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, and property losses. These categories are not automatic awards, and an impaired-driving allegation does not create a standard settlement amount.

Available insurance, fault disputes, evidence, and the responsible parties’ ability to pay affect the practical evaluation. The amount remaining for a client can also be reduced by fees, case expenses, and valid repayment obligations. Read compensation available after an accident.

If a family member died, different rules govern who may bring wrongful-death and related claims. See wrongful death after a vehicle accident for an introduction and seek an individual evaluation.

Are punitive damages available?

Punitive damages may be available in some cases, but they are not automatic after a DUI arrest or conviction. Civil Code section 3294 requires clear and convincing proof of oppression, fraud, or malice. An impaired-driving case may involve allegations of conscious disregard for others’ safety, but the specific facts and legal standard must be evaluated.

The California Supreme Court has recognized that qualifying intoxicated-driving conduct can support punitive damages. That does not mean every impaired-driving collision qualifies, or that an insurer will pay such an award. Coverage, legal restrictions, and collectability require separate review. Read Civil Code section 3294 and the Peterson decision discussing the Taylor rule, hosted by Stanford.

Could someone other than the driver be responsible?

Depending on the evidence, an investigation may examine vehicle ownership and permission, an employer’s connection to the trip, or negligent entrustment. Employment or ownership alone does not answer every liability question. Each theory has its own requirements.

Bars, restaurants, and social hosts

California generally limits civil liability for furnishing alcohol. It is not enough simply to show that a bar served an adult who later caused a crash. Narrow statutory exceptions can apply, including certain transactions involving an obviously intoxicated minor and an adult knowingly furnishing alcohol at the adult’s residence to someone the adult knew or should have known was under 21.

These exceptions have specific conditions and causation requirements. Preserve relevant facts and obtain advice rather than assuming that every alcohol provider can be sued. See Civil Code section 1714 and CACI 422 on alcohol provided to obviously intoxicated minors.

Restitution, victim assistance, and insurance

Criminal restitution

Victim restitution can address qualifying economic losses through the criminal proceeding. Keep records of expenses and payments, and ask the prosecutor’s victim-witness assistance office about the process. A restitution order does not guarantee immediate collection or necessarily address all damages potentially available in a civil case. The California Courts victim resources guide explains support and legal options.

California Victim Compensation Board

Eligible victims of qualifying crimes may receive help with specified expenses through CalVCB, subject to program rules and limits. It is not a replacement for all civil damages. Review eligibility and covered expenses.

Tell your lawyer about assistance received, restitution payments, and other reimbursements. CalVCB may have repayment rights and notification requirements when a lawsuit or insurance claim is filed. See its repayment guidance. Coordinate overlapping sources to avoid assuming the same expense can be collected twice.

Insurance options

Do not assume intoxication either guarantees or eliminates insurance coverage. Review the applicable policies and circumstances. If the at-fault driver’s insurance is insufficient or unavailable, uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage may provide options, subject to its requirements.

Before releasing a driver or accepting payment, review effects on other claims, coverage, and repayment obligations. See insurance settlement offers and releases.

Deadlines and working with MMG

California personal-injury lawsuits generally have a two-year deadline, but exceptions and shorter requirements can apply. Government claims often require an administrative claim within six months. Criminal proceedings and negotiations do not automatically pause civil deadlines. Review the California Courts personal-injury guide and California accident claim deadlines.

An MMG evaluation can identify records to preserve, potential recovery sources, approaching deadlines, and questions about the relationship between criminal and civil proceedings. If representation is agreed upon, the written agreement sets the scope and fee terms.

MMG advances case expenses without upfront payment. Contingency rates vary by case stage. No recovery means no attorney fees or case expenses owed to MMG; medical bills and other third-party obligations are separate. Read attorney fees and case costs.

When accounts conflict, the evidence matters

One driver says the light was green. Another says a turning vehicle crossed their path. After an intersection crash, the point of impact alone may not explain who had the right of way or whose conduct caused the collision.

What is a T-bone accident?

A T-bone collision generally describes the front of one vehicle striking the side of another. It can happen when a driver crosses an intersection, turns across traffic, or enters a roadway. Not every intersection crash is a T-bone collision, and not every side impact happens at an intersection.

Being in the struck vehicle does not automatically establish that you were fault-free. Being in the striking vehicle does not automatically establish that you caused the crash. The investigation must consider each driver’s conduct before impact, the traffic controls, and the available evidence.

First steps after an intersection collision

Prioritize safety and medical care. Call 911 for an emergency and follow responders’ directions. Do not walk into an active intersection to take photographs or search for evidence.

  • Exchange driver, vehicle, and insurance information when safe.
  • Record the intersection, travel directions, lanes, approximate time, and responding agency’s report number.
  • Photograph damage, road markings, signs, and the broader scene only from a safe position.
  • Obtain witness names and contact details without coaching their accounts.
  • Preserve original dashcam video, including footage before and after the impact.
  • Keep medical records, repair estimates, receipts, and insurer correspondence.

A photograph taken afterward can show the layout, but it does not necessarily show the signal phase at the time of the crash. Make that distinction clear in your notes.

California DMV requires a separate SR-1 report within 10 days when someone is injured or killed, or property damage exceeds $1,000. A police report does not replace it. Review DMV accident-reporting instructions and what to do after a California accident.

Traffic signals and right of way

Red lights, arrows, and permitted turns

The signal governing the driver’s lane and movement matters. A circular green light, a protected turn arrow, and a red arrow are not interchangeable. A permitted right turn on a circular red light generally requires a complete stop and yielding, and may be prohibited by posted signs. A red arrow prohibits the indicated movement. See the California DMV guide to navigating the roads.

Left turns across traffic

California Vehicle Code section 21801 requires a left-turning driver to yield to opposing vehicles close enough to present a hazard during the turn. The statute also addresses the duties of approaching drivers after the turning driver has properly yielded and signaled. A wave from one motorist does not establish that every other lane is clear. See section 21801 and CACI 704, the Judicial Council’s left-turn instruction.

Having priority still requires reasonable care

Right of way does not eliminate a driver’s duty to exercise reasonable care in the face of an apparent hazard. An investigation may need to address speed, visibility, attention, and the opportunity to avoid impact as well as signal color. Read CACI 701 on right of way.

Stop-controlled intersections, uncontrolled intersections, flashing signals, and signal outages require their own rule analysis. Do not assume that a rule for one setting decides another.

How can you prove who had the green light?

Conflicting statements are a reason to investigate, not to assume the case is unwinnable. Potential evidence includes original dashcam footage, nearby business or residential recordings, independent witnesses, and records from the agency responsible for the signals.

Ask promptly whether relevant footage exists and can be preserved. Some cameras only detect vehicles or provide a live view; they do not necessarily record. Availability, retention periods, access requirements, and usefulness vary.

Signal timing plans may explain how an intersection was intended to operate. They do not always establish exactly which indication was displayed at the collision time. Event logs, maintenance records, accurate timing, and qualified interpretation may be needed. A camera timestamp may also differ from the actual time.

Physical evidence can help test competing accounts: damage locations, final positions, roadway marks, and recorded vehicle information where available. That evidence must be interpreted in context rather than treated as a shortcut to fault.

What makes a witness account useful?

A helpful account separates what the witness actually saw from what they inferred after hearing an impact. Preserve contact information and tell counsel whether the witness was driving, walking, or looking from a nearby building.

Useful questions include which direction the witness faced, whether anything blocked their view, which signal they observed, and whether they saw the vehicles before impact. A statement that “the light was green” needs context: whose light, for which lane, and at what moment?

Do not suggest answers, edit original recordings, or pressure a witness to agree with your account. Preserve the collision report too; it may identify witnesses and observations even when its conclusions are disputed.

Side-impact injuries and medical evidence

The effect of a side impact depends on the actual collision and the person involved. Document where you were seated, the area of impact, restraint use, airbag deployment, and any intrusion into the occupant space, without guessing about what caused a particular diagnosis.

Seek appropriate medical evaluation and accurately explain symptoms, their timing, and relevant prior conditions. Medical records should guide discussion of head, neck, spinal, chest, or other injuries. Crash photographs and vehicle type cannot diagnose an injury or establish a person’s prognosis.

After a possible head injury, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness, or difficulty waking require emergency attention. Call 911 or seek emergency care. Review the CDC’s concussion symptoms and danger signs.

For lasting injuries, records of treatment recommendations, work restrictions, assistance needs, and day-to-day limitations can help document losses. Read about traumatic brain injury after an accident, spinal cord injury and paralysis, and medical bills and treatment costs.

Historical research. Individual circumstances.

The linked study uses 1999–2001 fatal-crash data. It does not predict your outcome or establish fault.

What the side-impact study tells us

The study you can read below examined paired passenger-car–SUV side impacts using 1999–2001 FARS data. It reported greater driver mortality odds for passenger cars in those selected crashes, with an overall matched odds ratio of 10.0 and a 95% confidence interval of 7.9–12.5.

That is not a current prediction that every passenger-car driver is ten times more likely to die in a side impact. FARS concerns fatal crashes, the vehicle fleet was historical, and an odds ratio is not an individual’s probability of death. In the authors’ analysis, adding vehicle weight explained nearly all of the car–SUV mortality difference.

The research provides context for investigating vehicle compatibility and crash circumstances. It does not establish fault, a particular injury, a vehicle defect, or compensation in your case. Read Driver Mortality in Paired Side Impact Collisions Due to Incompatible Vehicle Types and NHTSA’s explanation of FARS.

What if both drivers contributed?

California comparative-fault rules can reduce recoverable damages according to an injured person’s share of responsibility. A disputed turn and another driver’s unsafe speed may both require examination. A proposed percentage should be supported by evidence, not simply assigned because your vehicle struck the other car.

Read CACI 405 on comparative fault and our partial-fault guide. Passengers may have claims involving one or more responsible drivers; each person’s position should be evaluated separately.

Compensation, coverage, and settlement decisions

Depending on proof and applicable law, a claim may include medical expenses, future care, lost earnings, reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, and property losses. These categories are not automatic awards. Fault disputes, available insurance, and other recovery sources affect the practical evaluation.

The gross settlement amount also differs from what remains after attorney fees, case expenses, and valid repayment obligations. Explore compensation available after an accident and uninsured and underinsured motorist claims.

Before accepting an offer, consider unresolved medical needs and the rights a release would end. A property-damage discussion and an injury settlement are not necessarily the same agreement. Review the actual wording and see insurance settlement offers and releases.

Deadlines and your next step with MMG

California injury lawsuits generally have a two-year filing period, but exceptions and shorter requirements can apply. A potential government claim—for example, one involving a public entity’s alleged responsibility—often requires an administrative claim within six months. A signal issue does not by itself prove public-entity liability. Prompt review matters. See the California Courts personal-injury guide and accident claim deadlines.

An MMG evaluation can address preservation requests, disputed traffic movements, medical and financial records, insurance, and whether specialist investigation is warranted. If representation is agreed upon, the scope of work and fees will be set out in the agreement. No result is guaranteed.

What to do after a rear-end crash

Prioritize safety and medical care. Call 911 for an emergency. Do not enter moving traffic or put yourself at risk to photograph a vehicle. Follow emergency responders’ directions.

  • Exchange driver, vehicle, and insurance information when it is safe to do so.
  • Photograph vehicle positions, damage on every involved vehicle, road conditions, and nearby traffic controls if safely possible.
  • Save original dashcam files promptly, including footage before and after the impact. Keep an unedited backup.
  • Obtain witness contact details and the responding agency’s report number.
  • Seek medical evaluation for symptoms and describe when they began, what changed, and any previous relevant condition.
  • Notify your own insurer as required by your policy and retain correspondence, repair estimates, receipts, and claim numbers.

California DMV requires an SR-1 within 10 days when someone is injured or killed, or property damage exceeds $1,000. This is separate from a police or insurance report. Check the DMV’s SR-1 instructions. For a broader checklist, see what to do after a California accident.

California DMVMedlinePlusRear-end collision study

Is the rear driver always at fault?

No. Following distance is important, but responsibility depends on how the collision happened. California Vehicle Code section 21703 requires a reasonable and prudent following distance in light of speed, traffic, and roadway conditions. It does not make every rear impact an automatic finding of complete liability. Read Vehicle Code section 21703.

Drivers must also use reasonable care, watch for hazards, and control their vehicles. The Judicial Council’s motor-vehicle standard-of-care instruction, CACI 700, provides the legal framework. Evidence may show that more than one person contributed to a crash.

Common disputed situations

  • Stopped traffic: The investigation may examine following distance, attention, braking, and visibility. Stopping for traffic does not by itself establish fault by the front driver.
  • A recent lane change: Video, lane markings, timing, and witness accounts can help determine whether a vehicle entered the lane unsafely or the following driver failed to respond reasonably.
  • A chain-reaction collision: A middle vehicle may have been pushed forward, struck the vehicle ahead before the rear impact, or experienced multiple impacts. The sequence matters.
  • Disputed braking or vehicle condition: Claims involving brake lights, mechanical problems, or sudden stopping require supporting evidence; an accusation is not proof.

A police report can provide useful observations and leads, but it does not alone decide every civil liability issue. An insurer’s initial assessment can also be disputed with evidence.

Can you recover if you share some responsibility?

California comparative-fault rules can reduce recoverable damages by the injured person’s share of responsibility. Partial fault does not automatically bar a claim. Whether conduct contributed to the injury must be supported, rather than assumed from which vehicle you occupied.

For example, a dispute about following distance is different from a dispute about whether a vehicle was pushed into another car. Ask what evidence supports the proposed allocation. See CACI 405 on comparative fault and our partial-fault guide.

Evidence that can clarify your claim

The strongest record connects the crash sequence, your medical condition, and your actual losses. Different evidence answers different questions.

How the collision happened

Original video, photographs, witness accounts, scene measurements, vehicle inspections, and the collision report may help establish where vehicles were and the order of impacts. Vehicle data may be relevant when available and properly obtained; not every vehicle records the same information.

What changed medically

Treatment records, examination findings, recommended follow-up, and an accurate symptom history help clinicians evaluate your condition. Tell providers about prior injuries and distinguish earlier symptoms from changes after the collision. A preexisting condition does not answer every question about whether a crash caused additional harm.

How the injury affects daily life

Keep accurate notes about missed work, activity restrictions, assistance you need, appointments, and out-of-pocket expenses. Preserve wage records and medical recommendations supporting work limitations. Record facts without exaggeration or speculation.

Camera footage may be overwritten, and a vehicle may be repaired or disposed of. Raise preservation questions promptly. Coordinate any inspection with storage costs, transportation needs, and repair arrangements; do not leave a vehicle accumulating charges indefinitely without a plan.

Rear-end injuries need individual medical evaluation

Neck pain is one possible consequence, but a claim should follow the diagnosis and evidence rather than a label such as “minor impact.” MedlinePlus describes whiplash as a soft-tissue neck injury that can affect muscles and ligaments, with pain sometimes extending into surrounding areas. See its whiplash overview.

After a possible head injury, emergency warning signs such as a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, weakness, or difficulty waking require immediate medical attention. Call 911 or seek emergency care. The CDC’s concussion symptoms and danger signs also explain that symptoms may appear later.

Vehicle photographs document damage; they are not a substitute for a medical examination. Neither a small repair estimate nor a dramatic photograph, by itself, establishes the presence or severity of a particular injury. Medical and, when appropriate, qualified expert evidence must address the individual circumstances. For serious head-injury concerns, see traumatic brain injury after an accident.

RESEARCH WITH CONTEXT

Crash models are not a diagnosis.

The linked study models the trailing vehicle’s driver. Individual injuries need individual evaluation.

What collision research can—and cannot—tell you

A 2025 study by Liu and colleagues in Scientific Reports used computer crash models to examine how collision overlap and speed difference affected injury measures for the driver of the trailing vehicle. Overlap describes how much of the vehicles’ widths engage during impact. The modeled results varied with the collision conditions.

This was simulation research, not a clinical study of every person struck from behind. The authors identify limitations, including a lack of real-vehicle crash tests validating the study’s scenarios. Its findings should not be treated as a diagnosis, a universal safe-speed threshold, proof of fault, or a settlement calculator.

For a legal claim, the practical takeaway is to preserve crash-specific evidence and obtain individual medical evaluation. Read the rear-end collision study on PubMed Central or the publisher’s article.

What compensation may be available?

Depending on liability, proof, and available recovery sources, a claim may include medical expenses, reasonably supported future care, lost earnings, reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, and appropriate property-damage losses. These categories are not automatic awards.

Case value depends on the injuries, their consequences, disputed fault, available coverage, and other facts. A settlement’s gross amount also differs from the amount remaining after fees, expenses, and valid repayment obligations. Explore compensation available after an accident and medical bills, liens, and treatment costs.

If the other driver has insufficient insurance, your own coverage may provide options, subject to policy terms and legal requirements. Review uninsured and underinsured motorist claims before assuming there is no possible recovery.

Before speaking with an adjuster or accepting an offer

Be accurate, keep copies, and avoid guessing about speed, distance, medical prognosis, or legal responsibility. Ask who is requesting a statement and why. Your duties to cooperate with your own insurer can differ from requests made by another driver’s insurer; obtain advice before refusing a policy-required request.

Before agreeing to settlement, review what losses the offer addresses and which claims the release would end. Ongoing treatment, future needs, medical repayment claims, and other insurance benefits deserve attention. Do not assume you can reopen a completed settlement if symptoms worsen. See insurance settlement offers and releases.

California personal-injury lawsuits generally have a two-year deadline, but exceptions and shorter requirements can apply. Claims involving government entities often require an administrative claim within six months. Insurance negotiations do not automatically extend a filing deadline. Before you accept, understand what ends

A settlement offer can bring needed financial relief after an accident. It can also ask you to give up claims for injuries, future treatment, and losses you do not yet fully understand. Review the amount, the complete release, and your estimated net recovery together.

Have an offer or release in hand? Contact MMG Law Firm at (818) 539-7969 for a free case evaluation. Keep the document and every deadline. You can call even if your records are incomplete.

Your before-signing checklist

  • Get the complete offer, proposed release, and any attachments in writing.
  • Identify who will be released and precisely which claims will end.
  • Review ongoing symptoms, treatment recommendations, and reasonably supported future needs.
  • Compare the offer with documented losses, disputed fault, available coverage, and litigation risks.
  • Request a written estimate of fees, case costs, repayment obligations, and your net recovery.
  • Check whether settlement could affect other claims, including uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage.
  • Confirm acceptance deadlines, filing deadlines, payment terms, and any required approvals.

Do not assume you can cancel later. Before replying “I accept,” signing electronically, depositing a settlement check, or returning a release, obtain advice about the proposed terms. Depending on the circumstances, a binding agreement may arise before a formal paper release is signed.

USEFUL SOURCES

California settlement regulationCalifornia Courts

What is the offer actually paying for?

An offer may address vehicle damage, bodily injury, a particular insurance benefit, or several claims together. A payment for repairs does not tell you what a separate injury claim is worth. Equally, a document presented with a vehicle-damage payment may contain broader release language that needs review.

Ask the insurer to identify the coverage, claim, and losses included. Check whether the offer accounts for medical expenses, lost earnings, future care, reduced earning capacity, pain, and limitations on daily life where recoverable and supported by evidence. The amount demanded, the amount billed, and the amount legally recoverable are not necessarily the same.

Read more about compensation available after an accident and how an accident claim works.

Is the offer unreasonably low?

California’s claims-handling regulation prohibits insurers from attempting to settle claims through unreasonably low offers. Under section 2695.7(g), the Insurance Commissioner considers evidence about the insurer’s evaluation, including the claimant’s supporting records, relevant law, adjuster advice, liability, likely outcomes, and property-damage valuation. The regulation also addresses counsel’s advice about exposure above policy limits and distinguishes certain initial and final offers by claimant status.

A disagreement over value alone does not establish a violation. Identify what evidence was overlooked and why it changes the evaluation. Useful questions include: Which medical records were considered? What wage loss was allowed? What evidence supports the proposed fault percentage?

Read the California settlement regulation supplied for this guide, the Cornell reproduction of section 2695.7, and the California Department of Insurance regulation index.

A complaint and a lawsuit serve different purposes

You can seek help through the California Department of Insurance complaint process. A complaint does not guarantee a larger settlement or replace timely legal action.

California’s unfair-insurance-practices statute does not itself create a private damages action under section 790.03. Other remedies depend on the facts and applicable law. Claims involving your own insurer differ from claims against another driver’s insurer; a low offer does not automatically give you a bad-faith lawsuit against that driver’s insurance company. See the California Supreme Court’s Moradi-Shalal decision, hosted by Stanford.

What does the release give up?

A release is a legal agreement ending specified claims against specified people or entities. Read every page, including definitions and attachments. Ask for an explanation of language you do not understand before accepting it.

People and claims covered

Look beyond the named driver. The agreement may refer to employers, vehicle owners, affiliated companies, insurers, or broadly described additional parties. Determine whether claims against another potentially responsible person will survive. Confirm whether the release covers only property damage or also bodily injury and future losses.

Unknown claims and Civil Code section 1542

California Civil Code section 1542 generally protects certain claims unknown or unsuspected when a general release is executed. Settlement documents often expressly waive that protection. A waiver can affect claims involving consequences you discover later; it deserves particular attention when your medical outlook remains uncertain. Read Civil Code section 1542.

Do not assume that a new diagnosis or worsening symptoms will let you reopen an otherwise binding settlement. Whether a release can be challenged is a separate legal question requiring review of the agreement and circumstances.

Promises that continue after payment

Review provisions about liens, reimbursement, indemnity, confidentiality, dismissal of a lawsuit, and payment conditions. An indemnity provision may require you to reimburse or protect another party against specified claims. Ask who bears that risk and whether the wording can be clarified or narrowed.

The offer and your net recovery are different

The settlement amount is the starting figure. Your available proceeds may be affected by attorney fees, case expenses, medical liens, benefit-plan reimbursement claims, and other valid obligations. Some amounts may remain disputed or require a temporary reserve while they are resolved.

Request an itemized written estimate showing:

  • Gross settlement and any allocation between claims or recipients.
  • The fee percentage and how the agreement applies at the current case stage.
  • Case expenses and whether the fee is calculated before or after those expenses.
  • Each identified repayment claim, its status, and any negotiated resolution.
  • Any reserve, why it is needed, and what must happen before it can be released.
  • The estimated amount payable to you, clearly distinguishing estimates from confirmed figures.

At MMG, contingency rates vary by case stage and are explained in the written agreement. MMG advances case expenses without an upfront payment. If there is no recovery, no attorney fees or case expenses are owed to MMG. Medical bills and other third-party obligations are separate. See attorney fees and case costs and medical bills, liens, and treatment costs.

Timing, treatment, and other insurance

If you are still receiving care

Ongoing treatment does not automatically prevent settlement. It does mean that future care and uncertainty deserve careful attention. Discuss your prognosis with treating professionals and the legal effect of a final release with counsel. Do not delay medically necessary care to improve a claim.

If other coverage may apply

Before releasing an at-fault driver, review potential uninsured or underinsured motorist benefits and any policy consent or subrogation requirements. Other insurers may have rights affected by the settlement. Signing first and checking later can create avoidable disputes. Explore uninsured and underinsured motorist claims.

If a deadline is approaching

Ask for any proposed extension in writing, but do not assume it extends a lawsuit deadline. California personal-injury lawsuits generally have a two-year filing period; government claims can involve much earlier requirements, often six months. Exceptions and other deadlines may apply. Negotiations and an insurance complaint do not automatically pause the clock. Consult the California Courts personal-injury guide and our California accident claim deadlines guide.

Accept, counter, or continue the claim?

The decision should reflect the evidence, available recovery sources, release terms, likely time and expense, and your priorities. No universal multiplier or online calculator can resolve all of those questions.

A useful counteroffer connects a requested amount to specific evidence: a treating clinician’s recommendations, documented earnings loss, photographs, witness accounts, or a supported response to disputed fault. Preserve original records and the negotiation history. Avoid guessing, exaggerating losses, or making unsupported threats.

If agreement is not possible, discuss the available next steps and their risks. Litigation may be appropriate in some cases; it does not guarantee a better result. Learn about partial fault in a California accident.

COMMON QUESTIONS

Common questions about offers and releases

You may seek clarification, negotiate, or decline an offer, subject to the facts and relevant deadlines. There is no rule that every first offer is unfair, or that rejecting it will produce more money. Review its support and terms.

The regulation generally requires insurer payment or performance within 30 days after acceptance and any necessary properly executed release, subject to exceptions. That is not a promise that your net proceeds will reach you within 30 days. Payment conditions, required approvals, funds clearance, and unresolved obligations may affect distribution.

You can request an evaluation. Send the full document, acceptance communications, payment information, and relevant dates. Whether any claim remains or an agreement can be challenged depends on the circumstances. Do not assume a general cooling-off period applies.

Bring the offer, complete release, insurer correspondence, insurance information, medical bills, treatment recommendations, and any lien or reimbursement notices you have. Include the accident date and every stated deadline. Keep sensitive medical or financial records out of a general website message; ask how to provide them securely.

Partial Fault in a California Accident

Shared responsibility. Understand your options.

CLEAR ANSWERS. STRONGER TOMORROWS.

Partly at fault? You may still have a claim.

California generally reduces damages by your share of responsibility.

IN THIS GUIDE

An accusation is not the whole story.

Review what happened, what the evidence shows, and how each action contributed.

Can you recover compensation if you were partly responsible?

Yes, potentially. California generally uses pure comparative negligence in accident injury cases. Sharing responsibility does not automatically prevent recovery, even if your share exceeds 50%. Your damages can be reduced to reflect your own responsibility. You still need a valid claim against another responsible party.

The California Supreme Court adopted this approach in Li v. Yellow Cab Co.. The rule is a starting point—not a guarantee of payment or a substitute for reviewing the evidence, applicable law, and insurance.

How a fault reduction works

HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE

$100,000

Established damages

−

$20,000

20% share of fault

=

$80,000

Before other limits and deductions

Illustration only—not an MMG result or settlement estimate. Fees, costs, liens, coverage, and other rules may affect payment.

How a fault reduction works

For a simplified illustration, assume legally established damages of $100,000 and an injured person's share of responsibility of 20%. The comparative-fault reduction would be $20,000, leaving $80,000 before other limits and deductions.

$100,000 × (1 − 20%) = $80,000

These are invented figures to explain the arithmetic, not an MMG case result or an estimate of your case. Insurance limits, collectability, other legal rules, attorney fees, case expenses, and medical repayment obligations can affect what is actually received. Read more about medical bills and liens.

Your fault percentage and the value of your losses are separate questions. A percentage cannot tell you what your claim is worth without evidence of the damages and who is legally responsible for them.

What must support a claim that you share fault?

California's CACI 405 jury instruction explains that a defendant asserting the injured person's comparative negligence must establish negligent conduct and that the conduct was a substantial factor in causing the harm. An accusation alone is not proof.

Relevant questions include what each person did, what reasonable care required under the circumstances, and how the conduct contributed to the injury. The Judicial Council's official civil jury instruction collection includes CACI 405 and the related apportionment instruction, CACI 406. A readable reproduction of CACI 405 is also available.

Who decides the percentage?

During a claim, insurers and the people involved may disagree about responsibility. An adjuster's proposed allocation is a position to examine, not automatically a binding court decision. Settlement negotiations may resolve the dispute; if the case goes to trial, the factfinder evaluates the evidence under the applicable instructions.

Ask for the factual basis of a proposed reduction. Which actions are being alleged? What photos, witness statements, recordings, or other records support them? What contrary evidence was considered? Keep the explanation and related correspondence.

A police report can help an investigation, but it is not itself a civil judgment allocating damages. The absence of a citation also does not establish that someone was free from negligence. Tell counsel about any citation, hearing, admission, or prior decision so its particular significance can be assessed.

Examples of disputes that need closer review

One driver turned while another may have been speeding

An investigation may need to examine timing, visibility, signals, speed, and the opportunity to avoid impact. Neither the direction of travel nor one person's description determines the entire allocation. Video, vehicle positions, and witness observations may clarify the sequence.

Two vehicles changed position before a collision

Lane changes, merging, braking, or following distance may be disputed. Preserve the full recording rather than a selected clip; what happened before impact may matter. Avoid guessing at another vehicle's speed or distance when you did not observe it reliably.

A passenger is worried about the driver's mistake

Being a passenger in a vehicle whose driver may be responsible does not by itself establish that the passenger was negligent. Passenger claims need their own analysis, including potential claims against more than one driver and available insurance.

These are investigation examples, not predetermined fault percentages. Relevant questions can arise in car, truck, and motorcycle cases.

Preserve the facts that matter.

Contemporaneous evidence can make a real difference. Start by collecting and saving:

  • Original photos and video
  • Witness details and reports
  • Insurance letters and deadlines

Evidence that can help resolve a fault dispute

Preserve what is available without risking your safety or interfering with emergency responders:

  • Original photographs: vehicle positions, damage, road layout, signs, signals, visibility, and relevant road conditions.
  • Video sources: dashcams and nearby cameras; note the location and approximate time promptly because recordings may be overwritten.
  • Witness information: names, contact details, and what each witness actually observed.
  • Reports and correspondence: report numbers, diagrams, citations, insurer letters, and written explanations of fault decisions.
  • Injury and loss records: treatment records, work restrictions, receipts, and other documents supporting the claimed harm.

Keep original files and any available timestamps. Do not delete, edit, or selectively alter unfavorable material. If a vehicle may contain relevant electronic data, discuss preservation before repairs or disposal when feasible. The need for specialized analysis depends on the case.

What to do if an insurer says you caused the accident

Stay factual. Describe what you personally observed and say when you do not know. Do not guess at a legal percentage or change your account to fit what you think an adjuster wants to hear.

Ask for the decision and supporting reasons in writing. Keep a list of disputed points and documents that may clarify them. Before agreeing to a release or giving a detailed recorded statement to another party's insurer, consider discussing the request with counsel. Your own policy may require timely notice and cooperation, so do not simply ignore requests from your insurer.

Continue appropriate medical follow-up. Do not delay treatment to resolve a blame dispute. Keep any claim deadlines in view while discussions continue.

Partial fault is only one part of the legal analysis

More than one responsible party

Several people or businesses may have contributed to the harm. California distinguishes between categories of damages when allocating responsibility among defendants. For example, Civil Code section 1431.2 addresses several liability for noneconomic damages. A simple two-person percentage illustration does not resolve every multi-party case.

Insurance and other legal limits

A finding of fault does not establish how much insurance is available or whether a judgment can be collected. Separate rules may also restrict certain damages. For example, Civil Code section 3333.4 can limit noneconomic recovery for certain uninsured owners or drivers and certain drivers convicted of driving under the influence. Exceptions and the person's circumstances require review; lack of insurance is not itself a finding that the person caused the crash.

For an example of why the claim type matters, the California Supreme Court addressed a product-defect exception in Hodges v. Superior Court, available through Stanford's California Supreme Court Resources. That decision does not create a blanket exception for every uninsured claimant.

Filing deadlines still apply

California personal injury lawsuits generally have a two-year deadline. Public-entity claims can require an earlier administrative claim, commonly within six months. Exceptions and additional deadlines may apply. Ongoing negotiations or an unresolved fault dispute do not automatically extend the time to act. See the California Courts guides to personal injury cases and deadlines to sue.

Medical Bills, Liens, and Treatment Costs After a California Accident

Understand your bills. Know what affects your recovery.

PEOPLE  |  JUSTICE  |  RESULTS

A medical bill, an insurance statement, and a lien are different documents.

IN THIS GUIDE

Clarity before you pay—or settle.

Check the records, identify repayment claims, and understand the amount you may receive.

Understand the bills today—and what may come out of a settlement

After an accident, a hospital bill, an insurance statement, and a repayment letter can arrive for the same care. They may describe different obligations. Understanding the difference helps you ask better questions before paying a balance, signing a treatment agreement, or accepting a settlement.

MMG Law Firm offers a free case evaluation for California accident claims. Bring the bills and letters you have; you do not need to sort everything out first.

Call (818) 539-7969 or request a free case evaluation. Phone and video consultations are available. Glendale visits are by appointment.

Four terms that should not be confused

  • Medical bill: a provider's request for payment. The billed charge may differ from the adjusted amount, insurance payment, and remaining patient responsibility.
  • Explanation of benefits, or EOB: an insurer's explanation of how it processed a claim. It is not itself a bill.
  • Lien or reimbursement claim: an asserted right to payment from a recovery, based on a contract, statute, or other legal authority. Not every letter establishes a valid claim for its full stated amount.
  • Net recovery: the amount available to the client after applicable fees, case costs, resolved payment obligations, and any necessary reserves. It differs from the headline settlement amount.

Keep each document, including envelopes and deadlines. Matching dates of service and account numbers helps avoid confusing an unpaid provider balance with an insurer's request to recover money it already paid. The CMS guide to checking medical bills explains how to compare records and ask about discrepancies.

Who pays while the accident claim is pending?

Do not assume the other driver's insurer will pay each bill as it arrives. Liability, coverage, and damages may still be disputed. Your treatment funding and your injury claim can follow different timelines.

Depending on eligibility and policy terms, possible payment sources include health insurance, Medicare or Medi-Cal, automobile medical-payments coverage, workers' compensation for a work-related injury, or a provider payment arrangement. Each has its own requirements. Ask about network status, authorizations, deductibles, deadlines, and accident-related reporting.

Do not delay emergency care to discuss billing with a lawyer. For ongoing treatment, discuss medical needs with the treating professional and financial questions with the billing office and insurer. Tell your attorney promptly if cost is interrupting recommended care.

Your next step

Bring the bills and letters you have.

No recovery, no attorney fees or case expenses owed to MMG.

Medical bills and other obligations are separate.

Before you agree to treatment on a lien

Some providers agree to defer collection while an injury claim proceeds. A signed treatment-lien agreement may authorize payment from a recovery, but it does not necessarily make the care free if the case is unsuccessful.

Before signing, ask for written answers:

  • What are the charges, and will I receive an itemized statement?
  • Can available health coverage be used instead, and what changes if it is not used?
  • Do I owe the balance if there is no recovery or an insufficient recovery?
  • Are interest, finance charges, collection fees, or other terms involved?
  • Who must approve a reduction or release of the obligation?

A provider agreement is separate from MMG's fee agreement. Treatment choices should reflect medical needs; no settlement amount or bill reduction can be guaranteed.

Which repayment claims may affect the case?

Medicare conditional payments

Original Medicare may make conditional payments for accident-related care when another payer may be responsible. Those payments can become subject to recovery after a settlement, judgment, or other payment. Review the claimed services for accident-relatedness, report the resolution, and follow the applicable demand and dispute process. An interim conditional-payment figure is not necessarily the final amount. CMS explains Medicare's recovery process.

Tell counsel about all Medicare coverage, including Medicare Advantage or prescription plans, so potential obligations are identified. Do not assume one letter resolves every payer's rights.

Medi-Cal recovery

California's Department of Health Care Services has a personal-injury recovery process for relevant Medi-Cal payments. Reporting, payment review, and resolution can take time. Identify Medi-Cal involvement early rather than waiting until settlement funds arrive. Review the DHCS personal-injury lien process with counsel and request clarification of the services and amounts claimed.

Private health plans and other insurers

An insurer or health plan may assert reimbursement rights under plan language and applicable law. The type of coverage matters; a self-funded employer plan may raise federal-law issues different from a state-regulated insurance policy. Obtain the plan documents and payment breakdown rather than assuming every claim follows the same rules.

California Civil Code section 3040 addresses certain health-plan and insurer reimbursement liens. Its limits are not a universal formula for every medical lien. Applicability must be reviewed before calculating a reduction.

Providers and hospitals

A signed contractual lien, a hospital's statutory claim, and an ordinary unpaid bill are not interchangeable. Ask what authority supports the demand, what services it covers, what was paid or adjusted, and whether the asserted amount and notice comply with the rules that apply. A document labelled “lien” still needs review.

Check the bill before treating the balance as final

Request an itemized bill and compare it with the EOB and your records. Look for duplicate charges, services you did not receive, incorrect dates, missing insurance payments, or adjustments that were not credited. Ask the billing office to explain discrepancies and keep a written record of the response. CMS provides a practical billing-error checklist.

If you dispute a charge, ask whether collection activity will pause during review and request any agreement in writing. A dispute or pending injury case does not automatically stop every collection deadline. Never ignore a summons or legal notice; obtain advice promptly about the required response.

Some unexpected out-of-network bills may trigger federal or California protections, depending on the coverage and service. These protections do not eliminate every deductible, copayment, or medical debt. Start with CMS medical-bill rights and the California Department of Managed Health Care complaint process for plans it regulates.

Start with an itemized bill.

  • Compare insurance payments.
  • Ask about unexplained charges.
  • Request financial-assistance policies.

USEFUL RESOURCES

CMS: Your Medical BillsCalifornia HCAI: Patient Financial Assistance

Ask about hospital financial assistance

If a hospital balance is unaffordable, request its charity-care and discounted-payment policies and application. Ask what documents are needed and how a pending accident recovery affects the review. Eligibility is individual; do not assume that either insurance coverage or an accident claim answers the question by itself.

California's Hospital Fair Billing Program provides a hospital-policy lookup and a complaint pathway for financial-assistance issues. Hospital assistance may not resolve separate physician, ambulance, or other provider bills. Keep any written decision and tell counsel about adjustments so the accounting stays accurate.

Why reviewing medical debt matters

The December 2025 Harvard Petrie-Flom commentary Medical Debt is Bad, But Hospitals Make It So Much Worse criticizes hospital collection practices and draws attention to financial assistance and billing problems. It is policy commentary, not a California eligibility rule or a finding about your particular bill.

One underlying North Carolina State Health Plan report describes some nonprofit hospitals recording more than 60%, and even 80%, of bad debt against disadvantaged patients likely eligible for charity care. That is a specific finding about those hospitals, not proof that most California bills are wrong or must be forgiven.

The practical takeaway is to request the records, check the balance, and investigate assistance—not to assume a debt is valid or invalid from a headline.

Medical debt deserves careful review.

Harvard’s Petrie-Flom commentary examines hospital collection practices. California assistance rules require a separate review.

Understand the settlement accounting before you decide

Ask for an understandable estimate showing the proposed settlement, attorney fees under the agreement, case expenses, known repayment demands, unpaid bills to be resolved, and amounts still uncertain. A large settlement figure does not tell you what you will receive.

Gross recovery − attorney fees − case expenses − resolved payment obligations − any required reserves = estimated amount available for distribution.

This is an accounting illustration, not a valuation calculator. A reserve for an unresolved obligation is not necessarily a final expense; its later release or payment should be explained. Ask which figures are estimates and obtain written confirmation of agreed reductions or final balances. Avoid subtracting the same obligation twice.

For example, a provider's original charge, its adjusted unpaid balance, and a health plan's repayment demand may be three different numbers. The documents must be reconciled to determine what is actually owed and to whom. Read more about compensation after an accident and how an accident claim works.

  • Any treatment-lien or payment agreement you signed.
  • Collection notices, court papers, and stated deadlines.
  • Receipts, assistance applications, written reductions, and a list of your questions.

Use a secure method arranged with the firm for sensitive records. The initial website message should contain a short overview, not account numbers or detailed medical files.

Protecting your future starts with understanding your needs

A spinal cord injury can change how you move, work, travel, and manage everyday tasks. While your care team focuses on your health, legal questions may involve who caused the accident, how to document changing needs, and what resources may be available for the years ahead.

Suspected spinal injury is a medical emergency

After an accident, new weakness, loss of movement or sensation, difficulty breathing, or severe neck or back pain needs urgent medical attention. Call 911 if a spinal injury is suspected. Avoid moving the injured person unless necessary for immediate safety; follow the emergency dispatcher's instructions. Do not wait to speak with a lawyer. These examples are not a complete symptom checklist. MedlinePlus explains spinal trauma and emergency first aid.

What a spinal cord injury can affect

The spinal cord carries messages between the brain and body. Damage can affect movement, sensation, and body functions. An injured vertebra or painful disc does not, by itself, establish a spinal cord injury; diagnosis requires a medical assessment.

You may hear the terms paraplegia, affecting the lower body, or tetraplegia, also called quadriplegia, affecting the arms as well as other areas. Function varies with the injury. Clinicians use examinations and classification systems to describe its level and completeness. An incomplete injury preserves some function; these labels alone do not predict an individual's recovery. Read the NIH overview of spinal cord injury.

Ask your care team to explain the diagnosis, current restrictions, rehabilitation goals, and changes that need urgent attention. A legal claim should reflect your actual condition and needs, not assumptions based on a wheelchair, a scan, or a diagnostic label.
