AFTER A CALIFORNIA ACCIDENT

What to Do After a California Accident

Safety first. Clear steps for what comes next.

After a car, truck, or motorcycle crash, you do not have to solve everything at once. Start with immediate safety and medical needs, then document what happened, complete required reports, and preserve evidence. This guide explains practical next steps for California drivers, riders, and passengers.

Still at the scene? Call 911 for injuries or an immediate emergency.

Do not delay emergency help to gather evidence or contact a lawyer.

IN THIS GUIDE

YOUR IMMEDIATE PRIORITIES

Start with these six steps.

Do what you can safely. Missing records can be gathered later.

  1. 1

    Stop and address safety

    Call for emergency help when needed.

  2. 2

    Exchange information

    Collect driver, vehicle, insurance, and witness details when safe.

  3. 3

    Document the scene

    Save photographs, video, and factual notes without entering traffic.

  4. 4

    Get appropriate medical care

    Explain symptoms and follow the clinician’s instructions.

  5. 5

    Complete required reports

    Law enforcement, DMV, and insurance serve different purposes.

  6. 6

    Preserve evidence and check deadlines

    Keep originals and get advice about time-sensitive issues.

Once you are safe, request a free case evaluation or call (818) 539-7969. You can speak with MMG before every document is ready.

01

Stop, check for injuries, and get to safety

Stop at the scene. If anyone is hurt or there is an immediate danger, call 911 and give the location, travel direction, nearest cross street or exit, and known hazards. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.

For a crash with no injuries, CHP recommends moving the vehicle out of traffic to a safe location. Move only when it is safe; do not remain in a dangerous lane merely to photograph vehicle positions. If the vehicle cannot be moved safely, explain that to the dispatcher. Stay available to exchange information and speak with responders.

Do not walk into traffic to retrieve debris, approach a leaking vehicle, or chase a driver who leaves. Your safety matters more than a photograph. CHP’s traffic-crash guidance explains the immediate response.

02

Exchange details and identify witnesses

When it is safe, record each driver’s name, current address, contact details, driver’s license information, vehicle registration, license plate, and insurance company and policy information. Note the vehicle owner if different from the driver.

Ask witnesses for a name and a reliable way to contact them. Write down what you personally observed, including the time, location, direction of travel, lanes, weather, and traffic controls. Distinguish what you saw from what someone told you. Be truthful; avoid guessing about speed or arguing over fault. CHP explains what information to gather.

03

Photograph what you can safely document

Useful photographs may include a wide view of the location, each vehicle and its damage, license plates, lane markings, traffic lights or signs, debris, road conditions, and obstructions to visibility. Record the location of possible cameras on nearby businesses or homes.

Save the officer’s name, agency, incident number, and towing destination if available. If you leave by ambulance or cannot take photographs, focus on care. A trusted person may help obtain information later without putting themselves at risk. Missing scene photographs do not prevent an initial legal consultation.

04

Attend to symptoms and keep care records

Seek medical advice about pain, symptoms, or a possible injury, and follow the treating professional’s instructions. Tell them how the crash happened, when symptoms started, and whether symptoms have changed. Keep discharge instructions, referrals, bills, and appointment records.

Some concussion symptoms appear hours or days after an injury. After a head injury, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, confusion, or difficulty waking can require immediate emergency care. This is not a complete symptom list; use the CDC’s concussion symptoms and danger-sign guidance and obtain appropriate medical help. Do not wait for a lawyer to arrange care.

05

Keep law-enforcement, DMV, and insurance reporting separate

A police report, a DMV SR-1, and an insurance claim are different. Completing one does not automatically complete the others.

TASKTIMING AND NEXT STEP
Law-enforcement reportCalifornia DMV guidance calls for reporting to law enforcement within 24 hours if anyone is injured or killed. Contact the appropriate agency promptly and confirm what report has been made and whether anything further is required.
DMV SR-1File within 10 days if anyone is injured, however slightly, or killed, or damage to any one person’s property exceeds $1,000. Each driver has a reporting responsibility; a representative may assist.
Notify your insurerReport promptly and check the policy’s notice and cooperation requirements. Keep the claim number and adjuster’s contact information.

Read the DMV handbook’s collision instructions and DMV’s SR-1 requirements. Reporting requirements can apply even if you did not cause the crash or it happened on private property.

For a report prepared by CHP, follow CHP’s crash-report request instructions. If another agency investigated, request the report from that agency. Do not wait for the report before completing other required actions.

06

Preserve original evidence before it is lost

Create a private accident folder and keep an unchanged backup. The following practical steps help organize materials for later review:

  • Photos and video: retain original files, timestamps, and available metadata. Save dashcam footage before the device overwrites it; keep the original recording as well as any excerpt.
  • Messages and documents: keep texts, emails, insurer letters, estimates, tow receipts, and claim communications. Avoid deleting accident-related material, including social posts, before obtaining advice about preservation duties.
  • Vehicles and equipment: document where the vehicle, helmet, damaged clothing, or other items are stored. Before repairs, disposal, or a salvage transfer, ask whether an inspection is needed. Address storage charges promptly; preserving evidence should not mean ignoring accumulating bills.
  • Nearby cameras: note the address, camera location, approximate time, and business contact. Ask promptly about preserving footage and seek legal help when necessary. A preservation request does not guarantee access or require every recipient to provide footage.
  • Your losses: save bills and receipts and record missed work and changes in daily activities accurately. Keep dated notes without exaggeration.

California Courts identifies common evidence in injury cases, including photographs, medical records, witness statements, and police reports. Different evidence can answer different questions; there is no single document that proves every part of a claim.

07

Understand requests from insurers before responding

Identify who is contacting you and which insurer they represent. Your own policy may require cooperation, including supplying information or a statement. Requests from another party’s insurer can raise different issues.

Be accurate, say when you do not know, and keep copies of what you send. Ask about the purpose and scope of a recorded statement, medical authorization, or release before agreeing. If you are unsure, seek advice promptly without ignoring your policy duties or deadlines.

Before accepting an injury settlement, understand what claims the release covers and whether it resolves future losses. A vehicle-damage payment may involve different terms from an injury settlement. The California Department of Insurance’s accident guide explains claim investigations and statements. Use the current DMV sources above for SR-1 thresholds.

08

Take extra care with truck and motorcycle evidence

After a commercial-truck crash: safely record the company name, USDOT number, truck and trailer plates, and any separate trailer identification. Driver-duty records, dispatch information, maintenance records, and vehicle data may require prompt preservation. FMCSA requires covered carriers to retain ELD duty-status data and backups for six months; other evidence may disappear sooner, and exceptions affect which vehicles must use ELDs. That retention period is not a deadline to bring your claim. Read FMCSA’s ELD guidance and MMG’s Truck Accident Lawyer page.

After a motorcycle crash: preserve the helmet, protective clothing, motorcycle, and original helmet-camera or action-camera files. Photograph damage without modifying the equipment. Ask about inspection before repair or disposal, and do not reuse equipment that may be unsafe. Visit MMG’s Motorcycle Accident Lawyer page.

For other vehicle collisions, see MMG’s Car Accident Lawyer page.

09

Check legal deadlines early

Many California personal-injury lawsuits generally must be filed within two years of the injury. Claims involving public entities can require a government claim within six months, followed by additional deadlines. Exceptions may change the timing.

If a public vehicle, public employee, or road condition may be involved, flag that issue when seeking advice. Do not calculate your deadline from this overview or wait for an insurer to finish investigating. An inquiry to MMG does not pause a deadline. See California Courts’ injury guidance and government-claim instructions.

Questions people ask after an accident

What if I already left the scene?

Write down what you remember, save existing evidence, contact the appropriate agency about reporting, and notify your insurer promptly. If a reporting deadline may have passed, seek advice about your circumstances. Do not invent or backdate information.

What if the other driver fled?

Do not pursue them. Record the plate, vehicle description, direction of travel, and witnesses if you can do so safely. Notify police and your insurer promptly. Coverage may depend on policy terms and specific notice and proof requirements; do not assume a hit-and-run is automatically covered.

Do I need a lawyer for every accident?

No. Some straightforward property-damage claims can be handled directly with an insurer. Legal advice may be especially useful for injuries, disputed fault, multiple responsible parties, truck collisions, uncertain releases, or a possible government claim.

Can I call before I have the police report?

Yes. Start with the date, location, accident type, and your main concerns. If available, keep the report number and insurance letters nearby. You can ask for an evaluation while gathering the remaining records.

BROWSE QUESTIONS

24 practical answers

Before you contact a lawyer

The case evaluation is free, and you are not obligated to hire the firm. You can explain what happened, ask questions, and discuss whether MMG can help. An inquiry is an opportunity to understand your options; it is not a promise that the firm will accept the case or that you will recover compensation.

Not every claim requires a lawyer. A straightforward vehicle-damage claim may be manageable directly with an insurer. Legal advice becomes especially useful when you have injuries, disputed fault, an unclear settlement offer, several potentially responsible parties, or a deadline concern. A consultation can help you decide what assistance is appropriate. California Courts explains how a lawyer can help with a civil case.

Yes. You can ask for an evaluation without deciding for yourself whether your injury is “serious enough.” Explain when symptoms began, what care you received, and any delay or gap in treatment. Those facts can affect how the claim is evaluated. A lawyer evaluates legal issues; a healthcare professional should assess symptoms and treatment needs. Do not postpone appropriate care while waiting to speak with a lawyer.

No. Start with what you know. Share the accident date and location, the type of collision, a brief description, and a safe way to reach you. If available, keep the report number, insurer’s letters, photographs, witness details, and information about treatment. Missing documents do not prevent an initial conversation. Preserve original files and messages; wait for instructions before sending sensitive records.

Not by itself. MMG reviews inquiries, checks for conflicts, and discusses whether the firm can help. For an accepted contingency-fee matter, the firm uses a written representation agreement. Confirm whether MMG has accepted your matter and what work it will handle. An automated acknowledgment is not acceptance of your case. Read the Website Legal Disclosures.

Bring what you have.

You can contact us before every record is ready.

Fees & case expenses

Accepted accident cases are handled on a contingency-fee basis, with rates that vary by case stage. The written agreement explains the percentage, when each rate applies, how expenses are treated, and how deductions from a recovery are calculated. MMG advances case expenses without an upfront payment. Ask the firm to walk through the agreement before you sign; no standard percentage is quoted here because the applicable terms must be explained for your matter.

You owe MMG no attorney fees or case expenses if there is no recovery. That is MMG’s confirmed arrangement for its contingency-fee accident cases. Medical bills, liens, and other obligations to third parties are separate; those obligations are not automatically erased by the firm’s fee arrangement. Ask about both the representation agreement and any separate medical-payment agreement.

An injury claim does not automatically stop bills or collection activity. Possible payment sources include health insurance, applicable medical-payments coverage, or other arrangements, depending on your circumstances. Providers and insurers may have reimbursement or lien rights that affect the final distribution. Keep bills and benefit statements, and ask about payment responsibilities before agreeing to an arrangement. California’s auto-insurance guide explains medical-payments coverage.

Yes. Lack of health insurance does not prevent an initial legal consultation. Tell the firm about difficulties obtaining care and any bills or payment agreements. Ask providers about available financial assistance or payment options. MMG cannot promise free treatment, a particular provider, or that every medical bill will be covered by a recovery. Do not confuse a medical-treatment obligation with the firm’s no-recovery fee arrangement.

No recovery. No MMG fees.

Compare the fee, expense and third-party questions in one place.

Fault & insurance

Possibly. Being partly responsible does not automatically prevent a California negligence claim. Compensation can be reduced by your share of responsibility. For illustration only, a 20% fault allocation would generally reduce otherwise recoverable damages by 20%; that is not an estimate of your case. Fault depends on evidence, not simply what a driver or adjuster says. See California’s civil jury instruction 405 on comparative fault.

First identify whose insurer is asking and what it wants. Your own policy may require timely reporting and cooperation. Requests from another driver’s insurer present different considerations. Before giving a recorded statement, a broad medical authorization, or a detailed account while facts are uncertain, ask about your obligations and options. Be truthful and do not guess. The California Department of Insurance explains the claim investigation process.

An offer alone does not mean it is too late to ask for advice. Bring the offer and any release for review before signing. A release can give up rights beyond the immediate payment, and vehicle-damage and injury settlements may address different claims. If you already signed something or accepted payment, share the documents promptly so a lawyer can assess their effect. California Courts discusses legal help with settlement offers and agreements.

There may be coverage to investigate, but payment is not automatic. Depending on the policy and facts, uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage may help. Hit-and-run claims can involve special proof and reporting requirements. Preserve available evidence and promptly check applicable notices and deadlines. Read the California Department of Insurance’s explanation of UM/UIM coverage.

Deadlines & reporting

Many personal-injury lawsuits generally have a two-year filing period, but you should not assume that deadline applies to you. Injury claims against public entities generally require an administrative claim within six months, and other rules or exceptions may change the timing. An insurance claim is different from a lawsuit. Contacting MMG does not pause any deadline. See California Courts’ personal-injury guidance and government-claim guidance.

No. DMV reporting is a separate obligation. California DMV generally requires an SR-1 within 10 days when an accident causes injury, death, or property damage over $1,000. A report to police or your insurer does not replace the SR-1. You can contact MMG while gathering documents; do not delay a required report while waiting for a consultation. See DMV’s accident-reporting instructions.

Different deadlines. Different duties.

A reporting deadline is not the same as a lawsuit deadline.

Compensation, bills, and the case process

A reliable evaluation requires more than the accident type or a medical-bill total. Relevant issues include responsibility, the injury’s effects, documented losses, future needs, evidence, and available sources of payment. Depending on the case, damages may include medical expenses, lost earnings, and pain and suffering. A settlement amount is also different from the amount you receive after fees, expenses, and applicable liens. No recovery amount can be promised. California Courts outlines personal-injury claims and losses.

There is no dependable timeline before the facts are reviewed. Treatment, the availability of records, fault disputes, insurance coverage, negotiations, and any court proceedings affect timing. Ask what the next milestone is and what could delay it. A fast offer is not necessarily a complete assessment of your losses, but delaying a decision also has consequences. The appropriate approach depends on your circumstances.

Not necessarily. A claim may resolve through negotiation, and filing a lawsuit does not automatically mean there will be a trial. Litigation can still involve document requests, testimony, or other participation before a trial. MMG can explain the steps that may apply and discuss settlement decisions with you. California Courts describes settlement and other ways to resolve disputes outside trial.

Truck and motorcycle accident concerns

A truck claim may involve several businesses and evidence with limited retention periods. Driver logs, vehicle information, maintenance records, and other materials may need prompt preservation. FMCSA states that covered carriers must retain electronic driver-duty records and backup data for six months; other evidence follows different rules. That retention period is not your lawsuit deadline. See FMCSA’s ELD guidance and MMG’s Truck Accident Lawyer page.

Lane splitting does not automatically make a rider responsible for a collision. CHP recognizes lane splitting as legal in California. The circumstances—including speed, visibility, traffic, and the actions of everyone involved—still matter when fault is assessed. Preserve video, photographs, and witness information when available. Read CHP’s motorcyclist safety guidance and MMG’s Motorcycle Accident Lawyer page.

Keep the first form submission brief. Wait for instructions before sending medical records, identification documents, or extensive sensitive information. California privacy rights

California’s CCPA, as amended by the CPRA, gives eligible consumers rights concerning covered businesses. These include access, deletion, correction, opting out of sale or sharing, certain limits on sensitive-information uses, and freedom from discriminatory treatment for exercising rights. For covered businesses, California guidance generally specifies acknowledgment of access/correction/deletion requests within 10 business days and a substantive response within 45 calendar days, with a permitted extension on notice. Applicable sale/sharing opt-outs have a different timeline. See official guidance on requests. MMG’s published procedures must match the obligations and commitments that apply to it.

Protecting information

MMG’s existing policy describes reasonable safeguards for information held in its systems. Internet transmission and electronic storage cannot be guaranteed to be completely secure. Please use the initial form to share basic contact and incident information, and ask the firm how to provide sensitive documents appropriately.

If you believe information sent to MMG has been exposed or sent to the wrong recipient, contact the firm using the details above. Do not send additional sensitive details until an appropriate channel has been arranged.

Children and information about minors

The website is intended for adults seeking legal information or contacting the firm. It is not directed to children under 13. A parent, guardian, or other authorized adult may contact MMG about a minor’s injury; please begin with the adult’s contact details and a brief description rather than a child’s detailed records.

If you believe a child under 13 submitted information directly through the website, contact MMG so the situation can be reviewed.

External websites

Links to courts, government resources, maps, and other websites lead to services with their own practices. Review the destination’s privacy information before submitting personal details. A link to an authority does not imply that the authority endorses MMG.

Policy updates

The final published policy should display its effective date and last-updated date. MMG will identify revisions on this page and provide any additional notice required by applicable law. A new effective date will be assigned when the approved revision is published.

Statewide representation

An accident can leave you managing treatment, insurance calls, missed work, and questions about what happens next. MMG Law Firm represents injured people across California from its Glendale office, with attorney Mihran M. Ghazaryan personally handling their cases.

Established in 2018, MMG Law Firm was founded by Mihran M. Ghazaryan. The firm represents people injured in car, truck, motorcycle, and other accidents. Its solo-practice structure keeps the attorney directly involved in the work and conversations that shape each case.

Understand the person. Build the case.

We start with what happened, how the injury affects your life, and the questions you need answered.

The facts of a collision matter. So do the practical consequences: treatment appointments, time away from work, changes in mobility, and uncertainty about future care. A useful legal conversation addresses both.

We begin with your account of the accident and the information available. From there, the questions become more specific: What evidence supports the claim? What still needs to be obtained? Which issues are disputed? What decisions need your attention?

We explain options in plain language, including uncertainties. A case assessment should help you understand the choices ahead without promising a result before the evidence is reviewed.

Attorney Fees and Case Costs

No recovery, no attorney fees or case expenses.

MMG advances case expenses without an upfront payment.
Contingency rates differ by case stage. Your written agreement explains the terms.

Medical bills and other outside obligations are separate.

After a California car, truck, or motorcycle accident, you should understand the cost of legal help before deciding whether to hire a lawyer. MMG Law Firm handles accepted accident cases on a contingency fee basis and advances case expenses without an upfront payment from you.

Understand the three categories

Attorney fees

Payment for legal work.

A percentage of a recovery under your written agreement. Rates differ by case stage. No recovery means no attorney fees owed to MMG.

Case expenses

Costs of pursuing your claim.

MMG advances these expenses without an upfront payment. Your agreement explains how they are handled if there is a recovery. No recovery means no case expenses owed to MMG.

Outside obligations

Medical bills and repayment claims.

These are separate obligations. Their treatment depends on the bill, coverage, agreement, and applicable law. They are not automatically erased by MMG’s no-recovery policy.

Know what you’re agreeing to.

Rates differ by case stage. Review each percentage and its trigger before signing.

A contingency fee ties the attorney’s payment to a recovery. The percentage and calculation method belong in the written agreement. The State Bar explains that clients should understand whether the fee is calculated before or after costs are deducted and that fees are generally negotiable. Read the State Bar’s fee guide

At MMG, different rates apply at different case stages. Before signing, review each percentage and the event that triggers a change. Do not assume a single advertised percentage applies throughout a case. Your free consultation is the place to discuss the terms for your claim, including whether the agreement covers related matters such as property damage or an appeal.

MMG advances case expenses

No upfront payment. Your agreement explains reimbursement if there is a recovery.

Records and evidence

Medical records, incident reports, and other documentation.

Court filings and depositions

Filing fees, court costs, and deposition expenses.

Expert analysis

Independent medical and technical experts as needed.

Investigation and accident reconstruction may also be needed. Not every case needs every expense. Ask how expenses will be documented, how major expenditures are discussed, and how reimbursement works if money is recovered.

What happens if there is no recovery?

You owe MMG no attorney fees or case expenses if there is no recovery.

This answers what you owe the firm. It does not mean a hospital, medical provider, insurer, or another party automatically gives up a separate payment claim. Bring medical bills, insurance correspondence, and any payment agreements to your consultation so those issues can be discussed separately.

Before signing, also ask how the agreement addresses a change of attorney, early termination, or any court-ordered payment to another party. Those questions need answers specific to your situation.

Medical bills and healthcare repayment claims

Medical treatment bills are different from the costs of pursuing a legal case. Share your health coverage information and any lien or reimbursement notices early.

Medi-Cal

California’s Department of Health Care Services may recover payments for injury-related Medi-Cal services when a member receives compensation from a liable third party. The amount requires case-specific review.

DHCS Personal Injury Program

Medicare

Medicare may make conditional payments for treatment when another payer is responsible. A settlement or other recovery can trigger a repayment process.

Medicare’s recovery process

These sources explain the programs; they do not determine the amount owed in your case. Do not assume every medical charge must be deducted in full or that every repayment claim can be eliminated.

GOVERNMENT CLAIMS

A claim first. A lawsuit later.

Common California injury, death, and personal-property claims.

01

Present the claim

Generally within six months from accrual.

Identify the proper public entity. Keep proof of presentation.

02

Review the response

Generally 45 days for agency action.

Amendments and written extensions can affect timing.

03

Check the deadline to sue

Compliant written rejection: generally six months from personal delivery or mailing.

No compliant notice: generally two years from accrual, subject to exceptions and adjustments.

Keep every notice and its envelope.

The initial claim requirement still applies. Review any later notice promptly.

California Courts guidanceGovernment Code § 945.6

General information. This window does not calculate your deadline.

EXCEPTIONS & LATE CLAIMS

Some situations need closer review.

An exception depends on the facts and the applicable law.

An injured child

Private-party time limits may pause during minority. Government claim requirements are different; do not wait until age 18.

Later discovery

What you knew, and when you reasonably should have known it, can matter. A later diagnosis does not automatically restart the clock.

Legal incapacity

Specific statutory rules may apply. Receiving treatment or being unable to work does not automatically qualify.

A missed government claim

A late-claim application generally must be made within a reasonable time, not exceeding one year from accrual, with statutory exceptions. Relief is not automatic.

Treatment and insurance negotiations do not automatically extend a deadline.

General information. No deadline is calculated here.

Which insurance may respond?

Review coverage before assuming it applies.

Liability coverage

May apply when another driver or the motorcycle operator is at fault.

Uninsured or underinsured motorist

May provide coverage when the at-fault party has limited or no insurance.

Medical payments

May help with immediate medical expenses, regardless of fault.

Health coverage

Your own health insurance may also be a source of coverage.

Key questions to review

  • Who is insured?
  • What exclusions apply?
  • What limits are available?
  • Are multiple people claiming?

Policies cannot simply be added together.

CALIFORNIA LEFT TURNS

Who had the right of way?

A turning driver must yield to approaching traffic that presents a hazard.

After properly yielding and signaling, the turning driver may proceed; approaching drivers then have a duty to yield.

The turn sequence matters.

Read Vehicle Code § 21801

2023 RESEARCH REVIEW

Why injury can evolve after impact.

Spinal cord injuries can involve a range of complex biological processes. Research shows that some effects may develop or evolve after the initial trauma.

Primary injury

Initial trauma can damage spinal cord tissue and blood vessels.

Secondary injury

Biological responses after trauma can contribute to further damage.

Emerging research does not predict individual recovery or establish a universal cure.

Protein & Cell · 2023

Read the research review

Understanding consciousness after a TBI

After a severe traumatic brain injury, a person’s level of consciousness may change. Here are some terms families often hear.

Minimally conscious state

Limited but definite signs of awareness. A person may show inconsistent but purposeful responses to people, objects, or the environment.

Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome

Wakefulness without observable awareness. A person may have sleep-wake cycles and open their eyes but show no consistent signs of awareness.

Coma

Unconscious and cannot be awakened. A person does not respond to voice, touch, or other stimuli.

Brain death means the person has died.Qualified clinicians determine whether medical criteria are met.Read the NINDS guide

DEADLINES & REPORTING

Different deadlines. Different duties.

A reporting deadline is not the same as a lawsuit deadline.

Personal injury lawsuits

Many California injury claims generally have a two-year filing period. Exceptions can change the deadline.

California Courts guidance

Claims involving public entities

A government claim is generally due within six months for personal injury. Special procedures and exceptions apply.

Government claim guidance

California DMV accident reporting

An SR-1 is generally due within 10 days if anyone is injured or killed, or property damage exceeds $1,000. A police report does not replace it.

DMV reporting requirements

Have your specific deadline checked promptly.

INDEPENDENT GUIDANCE

California privacy rights

For eligible consumers dealing with covered businesses, California law provides rights that may include:

Know & access

Learn what personal information is collected, used, shared or sold about you.

Correct information

Request correction of inaccurate personal information.

Request deletion

Ask for deletion of your personal information, subject to certain exceptions.

Opt out of sale or sharing

Direct a business not to sell or share your personal information (for cross-context behavioral advertising).

Limit certain sensitive-data uses

Request limits on the use of sensitive personal information (for example, precise geolocation, health or biometric data).

Equal treatment

Receive the same level and quality of service, price and features even if you exercise your privacy rights.

Rights can have conditions and exceptions. A request does not automatically require deletion of every legal record.

BEFORE YOU CHOOSE

Questions to ask your lawyer

Bring these questions to your first conversation:

  1. 1

    Who will handle my case and be my main point of contact?

  2. 2

    How will I receive updates, and what response time should I expect?

  3. 3

    How should I raise an urgent issue or share sensitive documents?

  4. 4

    What are the strengths, uncertainties, and next steps in my case?

  5. 5

    How will attorney fees, case expenses, and other obligations be explained?

The State Bar recommends asking who will handle your matter, discussing the expected process and fees, and asking for simpler explanations when needed.
